title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
NoteNote for students taking the course in 2026–2027



For the 2026–2027 course, this chapter provides historical context and general background. Its historical content will not be examined. No examination question will require you to recall dates, names or historical details from this chapter.
Insurance is much older than the mathematics now used to study it. Communities shared losses, merchants transferred maritime risks and underwriters priced uncertain events long before probability had a formal language. The chronology is useful to keep in mind: institutions usually emerged because people faced concrete risks. Mathematics was then introduced, sometimes much later, to understand, price and manage those risks more systematically.
This is necessarily a selective history. The aim is not to identify a single birthplace of insurance, but to follow a few ideas that recur throughout the course: solidarity, pooling, risk transfer, information, diversification, reinsurance and the gradual use of probability and statistics.
Insurance also has a simple economic interpretation. It reallocates purchasing power across possible future states: the policyholder pays a premium in every state and receives an indemnity in some adverse states. The transaction does not create physical resources, and premiums must also cover expenses and the cost of capital. It can nevertheless increase welfare for a risk-averse policyholder because money is especially valuable after a loss. We return to this point in Chapter 2.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
1.1 Risk sharing before modern insurance

1.1.1 Reciprocity and solidarity
Exchange does not require an anonymous market or immediate monetary settlement. Within families, villages and other communities in which people know one another and expect to interact again, goods and services can circulate through reciprocity, gifts and informal credit. Anthropological work therefore gives little support to a universal sequence in which societies first relied on barter and only later discovered money and credit (Humphrey 1985).
David Graeber popularised the argument that barter was probably not the normal precursor of money within small communities. Where people knew one another and interacted repeatedly, exchange could instead rest on informal credit, reciprocity and obligations carried over time. Barter was more characteristic of exchanges with strangers or people unlikely to meet again (Graeber 2011). Graeber’s much broader historical narrative about debt and the origins of money is more controversial, however, and has been criticised on both empirical and interpretative grounds (Maurer 2013). The modest point needed here is much less contentious: repeated relationships allow obligations to be carried through time. Where people know one another, not every exchange has to be settled immediately.
Risk sharing can operate in the same way. A person or household struck by illness, fire, crop failure or death may be helped by relatives, neighbours or a wider community. There is no explicit premium and no calculation of an expected loss, but part of the shock is borne collectively. Informal solidarity is not insurance in the contractual sense, yet it provides an important conceptual precursor: losses that are severe for one person or household can be made more bearable when shared by many.


1.1.2 Pooling and maritime loans in antiquity
The ancient world gives more organised examples. Roman voluntary associations could combine religious, social and occupational functions, including assistance with funerals. Some collected contributions and used common funds to help members meet burial costs (Verboven 2019; Sakaguchi 2002). It would be anachronistic to call these associations insurance companies, but the pooling mechanism is familiar.
Long-distance trade created another problem: a voyage required substantial capital, yet shipwreck, piracy or seizure could destroy the venture. In the Greek maritime loan (nautikon daneion) and its Roman successor, the nauticum foenus, repayment depended on the successful completion of the voyage. Under the agreed conditions, the lender could lose the capital if the ship or cargo was lost (Ste. Croix 1974; Millett 1991).
Such contracts combined two functions that we now usually separate: financing the voyage and bearing part of its risk. The higher return in the successful state compensated the lender both for supplying capital and for accepting the possibility of losing it. Risk transfer was already present, but embedded inside a credit transaction.


1.1.3 Partnerships and trade in the Islamic world
From the early Islamic centuries onwards, commercial networks connected the Mediterranean, Red Sea and Persian Gulf with the Indian Ocean, East Africa, India and South-East Asia. Merchants used partnerships and agency arrangements to mobilise capital and organise trade across long distances. These financing arrangements could allocate commercial risk without taking the form of an interest-bearing loan (Udovitch 1970; Chaudhuri 1985).
An important family of contracts was the qirāḍ or muḍāraba. One party supplied the capital and another managed the commercial venture. Profits were divided in agreed proportions. In the absence of misconduct or negligence by the managing party, financial losses fell on the capital provider, while the manager lost the time and effort devoted to the venture (Udovitch 1970). These arrangements were not insurance policies, but they provided a way of allocating capital and commercial risk.
The prohibition of ribā, an Arabic word associated with increase or excess, helps explain why the form of a financial contract mattered. In Islamic jurisprudence, ribā covers prohibited gains in certain lending and exchange transactions. In the case of a loan, a stipulated addition to the principal in return for the passage of time falls within the prohibition. The concept is therefore not limited to an exceptionally high interest rate. It should not be confused with a prohibition of commercial profit or of every transaction involving deferred payment (Iqbal 1997). In a muḍāraba, the capital provider instead receives an agreed share of the profit actually made and bears the risk of losing capital.


1.1.4 Usury and finance in Christian Europe
Restrictions on lending also shaped commerce in medieval western Europe. The Latin Church’s prohibition of usury concerned a gain demanded merely by virtue of a loan, rather than only what we would now call an excessive interest rate. The Third Lateran Council of 1179 imposed religious sanctions on notorious usurers (Third Lateran Council 1179). In the thirteenth century, Thomas Aquinas argued that charging for the use of money lent, in addition to requiring repayment, amounted to charging twice for something whose ordinary use consisted in spending it (Thomas Aquinas, n.d.).
This did not make every return on capital illicit. Aquinas distinguished a loan from an investment in a trading partnership in which the investor retained the risk of loss. He also allowed compensation for certain actual losses caused by making a loan (Thomas Aquinas, n.d.). European merchants used partnerships and the commenda to finance ventures and share their results. The distinction between a loan and capital placed at risk therefore had practical consequences for the contracts they could use.
The doctrine and its legal treatment evolved unevenly. During the Reformation, Calvin allowed interest on some commercial loans under conditions of equity and charity, while other reformers remained more restrictive. Civil laws also began to distinguish permitted interest from payments above a legal ceiling (Munro 2011). Catholic teaching did not simply follow the same timetable. In Vix pervenit in 1745, Benedict XIV reaffirmed the prohibition of gain demanded solely by virtue of a loan, while recognising that other legitimate grounds for compensation or other types of contract could justify a return (Benedict XIV 1745).
These traditions should not be treated as identical, nor should legal doctrine be mistaken for a complete description of commercial practice. They nevertheless bring us back to questions that merchants faced across trading regions: who supplies the capital, who manages the venture and who bears the loss if it fails?

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
1.2 Insurance becomes an industry

1.2.1 Marine insurance as a separate contract
A major institutional step is visible in the commercial cities of fourteenth-century Italy, especially Genoa and Florence (Balard 1978; Piccinno 2016; Leonard 2016). Maritime risk sharing was not new. What changed was that risk transfer could be separated from the financing of the voyage.
A merchant who already owned a cargo could pay a premium to another party in return for compensation if specified maritime losses occurred. The insurer did not have to lend the merchant the value of the cargo. By the middle of the fourteenth century, surviving contracts contain the essential elements of recognisable marine insurance: a premium, specified risks, an amount exposed to loss and parties willing to bear that loss. The well-known Santa Clara contract from the 1340s is a useful example from this period (Botticini et al. 2023).
Risks could be divided among several underwriters. This limited each participant’s exposure and made information valuable: route, season, vessel, captain, cargo, piracy and war could all affect the price. Premiums were not produced by an actuarial formula. They came from experience, bargaining, reputation and what we would now describe as subjective assessments of risk.


1.2.2 The Low Countries and Lloyd’s
As European commerce expanded northwards, Antwerp and then Amsterdam became major centres of marine insurance. In 1598 Amsterdam established a specialised chamber to resolve marine-insurance disputes. Its responsibilities were extended later that year to disputes over general average, giving it the name Chamber of Insurance and Average (Go 2013; Go 2023).
Here average is a maritime term for losses or expenses and their allocation, corresponding to the French avarie. It does not mean an arithmetic mean. General average (avarie commune) concerns sacrifices or extraordinary expenditure deliberately incurred for the common safety of a maritime venture. If part of a cargo is thrown overboard to save a ship and the remaining cargo, for example, the resulting loss is shared among the interests involved according to the applicable contribution rules. The Chamber helped determine which losses qualified and how the contributions should be calculated (Go 2023).
This illustrates an important point: an insurance market needs more than people willing to take risks. It also needs enforceable contracts, brokers, conventions, reputation and mechanisms for resolving disagreements.
London later developed another influential market around Edward Lloyd’s coffee house. The first surviving public reference dates from 1688. Merchants, shipowners, captains, brokers and underwriters gathered there, and the coffee house became particularly valuable as a source of shipping intelligence (Lloyd’s, n.d.-a, n.d.-b). Risks could be shared among several subscribers rather than placed with a single balance sheet. Lloyd’s was therefore not initially an insurance company in the usual sense but a marketplace linking information, brokers and individual risk bearers.
The expansion of insurance accompanied the expansion of long-distance commerce. This is economically natural: transferring risk can make costly and uncertain ventures easier to finance. Insurance itself does not determine whether the activity being facilitated is socially desirable.






CautionHistorical note: insurance and slavery



Unfortunately, marine insurance was also part of the Atlantic slave economy. Underwriters, including participants in the Lloyd’s market, insured ships and commercial interests connected with the trade in enslaved people (Pearson and Richardson 2019; Draper, n.d.). This should be a reminder that a useful mechanism for transferring risk can also support activities that are morally abhorrent.




1.2.3 Fire insurance and prevention
The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed more than 13,000 houses and demonstrated the scale of correlated urban fire losses (London Fire Brigade, n.d.-b). Commercial fire insurance expanded in the following decades. Nicholas Barbon’s Fire Office was established in 1680 (London Fire Brigade, n.d.-a).
Insured buildings often displayed metal fire marks, and insurers maintained firefighting teams. These brigades had an obvious incentive to limit the spread of fire: an unchecked blaze could damage many insured properties at once. Contrary to a popular story, there is little evidence that insurance brigades routinely allowed uninsured or rival-insured buildings to burn. Cooperation was often in their common interest (London Fire Brigade, n.d.-a).
Early fire insurance already displays several recurring themes of non-life insurance: pooling many exposures, classifying risks, recognising accumulation and investing in prevention as well as compensation.


1.2.4 Life assurance and actuarial valuation
Life assurance is not the subject of the rest of this course, but it is historically important because life-contingent payments became one of the first areas in which probabilistic calculation was used systematically. Life assurance existed before such pricing. The Amicable Society, founded in London in 1706, operated a genuine life-assurance pool without initially charging age-specific premiums derived from mortality tables (Ogborn 1962).
The intellectual ingredients accumulated gradually. John Graunt’s analysis of the London Bills of Mortality in 1662 was a landmark in quantitative demography (Graunt 1662; Sutherland 2005). Edmond Halley used mortality data from Breslau in 1693 to construct a life table and calculate values for life annuities (Halley 1693). Abraham de Moivre developed methods for life-contingent calculations, and James Dodson later argued for premiums that varied systematically with age.
The Society for Equitable Assurances on Lives and Survivorships, founded in 1762, became an important landmark in long-term life assurance based on age-dependent premiums and mathematical valuation. Richard Price and William Morgan subsequently helped institutionalise regular actuarial valuation (Ogborn 1962; Society of Actuaries, n.d.). The broad lesson is simple: life assurance came first, and mortality statistics and probability then changed how it could be priced and managed.






NoteA related instrument: the tontine



Tontines sit between public finance, annuities and longevity risk rather than ordinary indemnity insurance. In the schemes associated with Lorenzo Tonti in the seventeenth century, payments became concentrated among surviving participants. They are worth remembering as another early attempt to organise financial contracts around uncertain lifetimes (Hellwege 2018).




1.2.5 Industrialisation, reinsurance and the state
The eighteenth and nineteenth centuries created larger concentrations of capital in factories, warehouses, railways, steamships and dense cities. Insurance became part of the infrastructure of industrial investment. Fire insurers gathered information on construction and industrial processes and increasingly differentiated premiums according to observable characteristics (Pearson 2004). New lines of business appeared as technology and liability changed: accident, engineering and employers’ liability were later joined by motor, aviation and many others (Borscheid and Haueter 2012).
Large accumulations of risk also made the limits of a single insurer more obvious. Reinsurance allows an insurer to pass part of its own exposure to another risk bearer. The Hamburg fire of 1842 helped stimulate the creation of Cologne Re in 1846, the first independent professional reinsurance company. The Glarus fire of 1861 was an important background to the foundation of Swiss Re in 1863 (Borscheid et al. 2013; Swiss Re, n.d.). The basic architecture remains with us: households and firms transfer risk to insurers, and insurers transfer part of that risk to reinsurers and capital markets.
Industrialisation and wage labour also changed the political treatment of risk. Germany under Bismarck is a major landmark: legislation in the 1880s introduced compulsory schemes for sickness, industrial accidents, invalidity and old age (Hennock 2007). During the twentieth century, welfare states expanded social insurance and governments increasingly required some private cover, notably motor third-party liability.
The state consequently appears in several roles: regulator, provider of social insurance, purchaser of insurance, authority making some cover compulsory and, for exceptional risks, backstop or reinsurer of last resort. Catastrophes and other highly correlated losses often make the boundary between private and public risk bearing particularly visible.


1.2.6 Insurance today
Insurance is now a layered international system. Individuals, households and firms buy cover from insurers. Insurers diversify and use reinsurance, while reinsurers distribute major risks across countries and capital providers. Governments regulate solvency and market conduct and may intervene when losses are too concentrated for private balance sheets alone.
The range of insured risks has also widened enormously: property and marine insurance coexist with liability, motor, aviation, natural catastrophes, business interruption, cyber risk and many other lines. Yet the central questions are recognisable throughout the history of insurance: which risks should be pooled, how should they be priced, how dependent are the losses, how much capital is needed, and who ultimately bears the most extreme losses?

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: 1.3 Insurance and the development of mathematics
text:
1.3 Insurance and the development of mathematics

1.3.1 From games of chance to probability theory
For most of the history above, underwriters worked without a formal mathematical theory of probability. That did not mean they ignored uncertainty. They compared routes and vessels, observed claims, negotiated prices and diversified. Their judgements were probabilistic in spirit, but based primarily on experience and market information.
The mathematical calculus of probability initially developed largely through questions about games of chance. Pascal and Fermat’s correspondence in 1654 addressed, among other problems, the problem of points: how should players divide the stakes if a game is interrupted before either has won? The division should reflect their remaining chances of winning (Hald 1990).
During a visit to Paris in 1655, Christiaan Huygens learnt of the problems discussed by the French mathematicians, without learning their methods. He developed his own approach after returning to the Netherlands. His treatise was published in Latin in 1657 as De ratiociniis in ludo aleae, translated by Frans van Schooten from Huygens’s Dutch manuscript (Huygens 1920). Its starting point was the fair monetary value of a chance of winning. Huygens asked what a player’s position in a game was worth, whether the stakes were to be divided or the position sold to someone else. For example, he valued an equal chance of receiving 3 or 7 monetary units at 5. Expectation thus emerged here as a way of valuing uncertain payoffs through fair games (Huygens 1657). This valuation rule should be distinguished from the willingness to pay of a risk-averse individual, which we study in Chapter 2.
Jacob Bernoulli’s Ars Conjectandi, published posthumously in 1713, contained the first proof of a law of large numbers (Mattmüller 2014). Pooling, however, did not wait for Bernoulli. The theorem provided a mathematical explanation for a stabilising effect that mutual groups and insurers could already observe in practice.
During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, de Moivre and Laplace developed normal approximations and limit arguments that became part of the history of the central limit theorem (Hald 1990, 1998). Much later, probability was placed on increasingly formal foundations. Borel helped bring probability into the emerging language of measure and integration in France, while the Russian school made major contributions through figures such as Chebyshev, Markov, Khinchin and ultimately Kolmogorov. Kolmogorov’s 1933 axioms gave probability the measure-theoretic framework still used today (Cléry and Mazliak 2022; Kolmogorov 1933; Plato 2005).
This history matters because actuarial practice and probability theory should not be confused. Insurance existed before probability theory, and the foundations of probability were not developed simply in order to solve insurance problems. The two histories eventually met and strongly influenced one another.


1.3.2 When practical problems generate mathematics
Practical problems in insurance and risk management have given rise to important mathematical questions.
A first example comes from Scandinavia. Filip Lundberg, working as both an actuary and insurance executive, studied the evolution of an insurer’s surplus and the possibility of ruin in his 1903 doctoral work. Harald Cramér later developed these ideas into a central part of collective risk theory (Cramér 1969). The underlying business question is immediate: how much capital does an insurer need to withstand the random timing and size of claims? Knowing the average cost of claims does not answer it.
A second example comes from the Netherlands. The North Sea flood of 1953 killed more than 1,800 people in the Netherlands and caused enormous damage. Dutch authorities then had to decide how strong sea defences should be when the relevant extreme water levels might occur only very rarely. David van Dantzig formulated the problem in explicitly statistical and economic terms, balancing the probability and consequences of flooding against the cost of stronger protection (Dantzig 1956).
This demand for extrapolation beyond ordinary observations remained a practical statistical problem. Decades later, Dutch extreme-value specialists, including Laurens de Haan, worked with public agencies on estimates of very rare sea levels used in coastal protection (Dillingh et al. 1993; Haan and Ronde 1998). The point is not that extreme-value theory was invented by the Dutch because of dykes. It is that a real problem of public risk management created a sustained demand for better extreme-value methods and brought mathematical statistics directly into engineering decisions.
Lundberg’s ruin theory and Dutch flood protection therefore illustrate the same broad mechanism: a practical problem comes first, and mathematics develops in response to the needs of decision-making under uncertainty.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
1.4 A historical perspective

1.4.1 A short timeline







Period
Selected development




Antiquity
Mutual associations share some large household expenses. Maritime loans combine finance and risk bearing


Medieval centuries
Long-distance trading networks use partnerships and other financing arrangements across Europe, the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean world


Fourteenth century
Separate marine insurance contracts are documented in Italian commercial cities


Sixteenth–seventeenth centuries
Antwerp and Amsterdam become major insurance centres. Lloyd’s coffee house emerges in London, and fire insurance expands after 1666


Seventeenth–eighteenth centuries
Pascal, Fermat, Huygens, Graunt, Halley, and Bernoulli provide demographic and probabilistic tools later absorbed by insurance


Eighteenth–nineteenth centuries
Actuarial life assurance, industrial insurance and professional reinsurance expand


Late nineteenth–twentieth centuries
Social insurance and compulsory cover grow. Probability becomes a formal mathematical discipline


1903 onwards
Lundberg and Cramér develop collective risk and ruin theory


After 1953
Dutch flood protection becomes an important application of probabilistic decision-making and extreme-value statistics





1.4.2 What to retain
The main lessons are that insurance precedes probability theory, that pooling and diversification were practices before they were theorems, and that separating financing from risk transfer allowed insurance to become a specialised activity. Mathematics then entered insurance from several directions: demographic statistics and probability provided tools for pricing and aggregation, while practical problems such as insurer ruin and flood protection generated new mathematical work of their own.


1.4.3 Further reading
For a broad international history, see Borscheid and Haueter’s World Insurance (Borscheid and Haueter 2012). Leonard’s edited volume is useful on the origins and diffusion of marine insurance (Leonard 2016), while Pearson gives a detailed account of British fire insurance and industrialisation (Pearson 2004). Hald provides a technical history of probability and statistics before 1750 and from 1750 to 1930 (Hald 1990, 1998). For the Dutch flood case, Van Dantzig’s paper is unusually readable as an example of a real public-policy problem being translated into probabilistic and economic terms (Dantzig 1956).

title: Reading
text: No single book covers the whole course. The list below is deliberately short: each title is particularly useful for one or more chapters, and together they provide a good route through most of the material.

title: Reading
text:
Notes on the list
Denuit and Charpentier’s two volumes (Denuit and Charpentier 2004, 2005) are the main references for Chapters 3 to 6 of the course. Volume I, Principes fondamentaux de théorie du risque, in particular, covers premium principles, risk measures and dependence structures. The books are written in French and assume little beyond a solid grounding in probability, making them unusually approachable introductions to a technical literature.
Henriet and Rochet (Henriet and Rochet 1991) is the main reference for Chapter 2. It is short and precise, covering the supply of and demand for insurance and then adverse selection and moral hazard. If you read one book alongside the lectures on contract design, make it this one.
Deelstra and Plantin (Deelstra and Plantin 2014) is a concise volume covering premium calculation principles and the institutional reality of the reinsurance market. It is the English-language complement to Chapters 3 to 5 and is particularly useful because it does not separate the mathematics from the market it describes.
Eeckhoudt, Gollier and Schlesinger (Eeckhoudt et al. 2005) is a standard modern treatment of decision-making under risk. Read it for the foundations of Chapter 2, and because it connects insurance with the broader field of financial economics.
Borscheid and Haueter (Borscheid and Haueter 2012) is an edited history of the global insurance industry from the late eighteenth century onwards, with chapters devoted to a wide range of countries. It provides useful background reading for Chapter 1. It is a long book, and you are certainly not expected to read it from cover to cover.

title: Insurance pricing and risk measures
text:
The previous chapters gave the pure premium a precise meaning. If the insurer’s payment is \(X\), its pure premium is the expectation of \(X\), computed under the relevant conditional distribution when observable characteristics are used for pricing. Throughout this chapter, that pricing information is understood to be fixed.
Charging the pure premium balances premium income and claims in expectation. Risk pooling makes the average claim more predictable, but it leaves the insurer exposed to fluctuations in total claims. The central limit theorem makes the distinction explicit: for independent claims with the same distribution and finite, positive variance, the probability that total claims exceed pure-premium income tends to one half as the portfolio grows. How should a premium reflect the uncertainty that remains?
One possibility is to charge
\[
\pi(X)=\lambda\mathbb E[X]=(1+\tau)\mathbb E[X],
\] where \(\tau\geq0\), or to add a fixed amount to the expectation. We keep the notation of Chapter 2: \(\lambda=1+\tau\) is the premium multiplier and \(\tau\geq0\) is the safety loading rate. Other loading coefficients will be denoted by \(\eta\). Before choosing a formula, however, we should distinguish expenses, which arise even when claims are perfectly predictable, from a safety loading associated with bearing risk. A commercial premium may also need to remunerate the capital committed to the business. These ingredients need not follow the same mathematical rule.
A loading based only on the mean gives the same price to
\[
\begin{gathered}
X=100\quad\text{almost surely},\\
\mathbb P(Y=10000)=0.01
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathbb P(Y=0)=0.99.
\end{gathered}
\]
Both payments have expectation \(100\), but their variances are \(0\) and \(990\,000\). The insurer knows the first payment in advance. The second usually costs nothing but occasionally requires a much larger payment. What feature of their distributions should distinguish their safety loadings?
A natural attempt is
\[
\pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\eta\sqrt{\mathbb V(X)},
\] where \(\eta\geq0\).
The standard deviation measures dispersion in the same monetary unit as the claim. But does this formula behave as we would wish when a payment increases, when contracts are combined, or when a small probability is attached to a very large loss?
We begin with premium principles, rules assigning a price \(\pi(X)\) to a claim, and examine classical examples through such questions. We then return to the construction of actual tariffs and to the important role of the insurer’s existing portfolio. This leads to a related but distinct problem: how to assess the aggregate losses that available financial resources should be able to absorb. Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall will provide two answers, whose interpretation, aggregation properties and computation we shall investigate.


Initially, \(X\) denotes a non-negative claim. A principle must be defined on an appropriate class of claims: integrable claims for the expectation, square-integrable claims for variance-based formulas, and sometimes a smaller class. Every statement below is understood whenever its arguments belong to the relevant domain.
The following properties are natural candidates. They are a list of objectives to discuss, rather than a claim that every commercial premium must satisfy every one of them.

Law invariance. If \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same distribution, then \(\pi(X)=\pi(Y)\). The premium depends only on the distribution of the claim.
Normalisation and exact pricing of certain payments. We would like \(\pi(0)=0\) and \(\pi(c)=c\) for a deterministic payment \(c\geq0\). There is no uncertainty to remunerate. Explicit administrative expenses can be added separately.
Non-negative safety loading. We would like
\[
\pi(X)\geq\mathbb E[X].
\]
Otherwise the expected underwriting result is negative even before expenses. Strict inequality for every non-constant claim is a stronger requirement.
Monotonicity. If \(X\leq Y\) almost surely, then
\[
\pi(X)\leq\pi(Y).
\]
A contract that never pays more should not cost more under the same principle.
Cash additivity, also called translation equivariance and often termed translation invariance in the risk-measure literature. For a deterministic amount \(c\),
\[
\pi(X+c)=\pi(X)+c.
\]
Adding a certain payment changes the premium by that amount. Together with normalisation, this implies exact pricing of certain payments. For non-negative claims, shifts must keep the claim in the domain. Later, with real-valued losses, we allow all real shifts.
Positive homogeneity. For \(a\geq0\),
\[
\pi(aX)=a\pi(X).
\]
Scaling every payment by the same factor scales its premium accordingly.
Subadditivity. For two claims on the same probability space,
\[
\pi(X+Y)\leq\pi(X)+\pi(Y).
\]
Combining risks should not cost more than pricing them separately. This is a weak diversification requirement: it does not require a strict benefit, and it must hold whatever the dependence between the two claims.
Convexity. For \(\theta\in[0,1]\),
\[
\pi(\theta X+(1-\theta)Y)
\leq\theta\pi(X)+(1-\theta)\pi(Y).
\]
Mixing exposures should not increase the premium beyond the corresponding mixture of premiums. Positive homogeneity and subadditivity together imply convexity. Conversely, convexity together with positive homogeneity implies subadditivity.







NoteA premium is not just a list of axioms



A fixed administrative fee breaks normalisation. A percentage expense allowance can break cash additivity. A loading for concentration may break homogeneity. These observations do not make such commercial charges illegitimate. They explain why we should distinguish a mathematical rule for the risk component from the final price of a contract.





The simplest loaded principle is
\[
\pi(X)=\lambda\mathbb E[X]=(1+\tau)\mathbb E[X],
\] where \(\tau>0\).
It is monotone, positively homogeneous and additive, even for dependent risks. For non-negative claims it has a non-negative loading. However,
\[
\pi(X+c)=\pi(X)+(1+\tau)c,
\]
so it is not cash additive and charges a loading even on certain payments. It also gives exactly the same premium to every claim with the same expectation.
The pure premium, obtained with \(\tau=0\), satisfies all the principal algebraic properties above. Its limitation is economic: it contains no safety loading. Good axioms alone do not force a substantial margin for uncertainty.



For \(X\in L^2\), set
\[
\pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\eta\sqrt{\mathbb V(X)},
\] where \(\eta>0\).
This principle is cash additive, positively homogeneous, exact on constants and at least as large as the expectation. It is also subadditive, because the triangle inequality in \(L^2\) gives
\[
\sqrt{\mathbb V(X+Y)}
=\left\|(X-\mathbb E[X])+(Y-\mathbb E[Y])\right\|_2
\leq\sqrt{\mathbb V(X)}+\sqrt{\mathbb V(Y)}.
\]
Consequently, it is convex. For independent non-constant risks, the square root in the loading produces a strict pooling benefit.
Its defect is more surprising: it need not be monotone. Let \(X\) take values \(0\) and \(1\), with probabilities \(p\) and \(1-p\), and let \(Y=1\). Then \(X\leq Y\), but
\[
\pi(X)=1-p+\eta\sqrt{p(1-p)}>1=\pi(Y)
\quad\text{if}\quad
0<p<\frac{\eta^2}{1+\eta^2}.
\]
For every \(\eta>0\), such a \(p\) exists. The principle can therefore charge more for a claim than its maximum possible payment. Indeed, monotonicity and exactness on constants together would imply \(0\leq\pi(X)\leq M\) whenever \(0\leq X\leq M\). Here the certain payment \(Y=1\) dominates \(X\) in every state, yet receives a lower premium.



Another classical choice is
\[
\pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\eta\mathbb V(X),
\] where \(\eta>0\).
It is exact on constants, cash additive and has a non-negative safety loading. Variance is convex as a functional on \(L^2\), so this principle is convex. It is also additive for independent risks, since
\[
\pi(X+Y)-\pi(X)-\pi(Y)=2\eta\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).
\]
This identity displays the failure of general subadditivity: taking \(Y=X\) with \(\mathbb V(X)>0\), we indeed have \(\pi(X+Y)-\pi(X)-\pi(Y) = 2 \eta \mathbb V(X) >0\). Positive homogeneity fails as well since
\[
\pi(aX)=a\mathbb E[X]+\eta a^2\mathbb V(X).
\]
Monotonicity also fails. Let \(a>0\) and \(p\in(0,1)\). Suppose that \(X\) equals \(0\) with probability \(p\) and \(a\) otherwise, and let \(Y=a\). Then \[
\pi(X)-\pi(Y)=ap\bigl(\eta a(1-p)-1\bigr)>0
\quad\text{when}\quad
\eta a(1-p)>1.
\]
Thus, using a variance loading does not resolve the problem encountered with the standard deviation.



The microeconomic chapter suggests another approach. Let \(u\) be continuous, increasing and concave on its wealth interval, let \(X\in L^1\) be a non-negative loss, and let \(w\) be initial wealth. The certainty equivalent of terminal wealth \(w-X\) is
\[
u^{-1}\!\left(\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\right).
\]
The corresponding certainty-equivalent premium for full insurance is
\[
\pi_w(X)=w-u^{-1}\!\left(\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\right).
\]
It solves
\[
u(w-\pi_w(X))=\mathbb E[u(w-X)].
\]
This is the largest premium that this policyholder would pay to replace the loss by a certain payment. Assume that terminal wealth remains in the domain of \(u\), that the expectation is finite, and that the inverse is well defined at that expectation.
Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\leq u(w-\mathbb E[X]),
\quad\text{hence}\quad
\pi_w(X)\geq\mathbb E[X].
\]
The rule is monotone and exact on constants. However, its other properties depend on the utility function, and it generally depends on initial wealth.
CARA utility. For \(u(z)=-e^{-\gamma z}\), with \(\gamma>0\), the dependence on wealth disappears:
\[
\pi(X)=\frac1\gamma\log\mathbb E[e^{\gamma X}].
\]
For this CARA calculation, utility is defined on all of \(\mathbb R\), so negative terminal wealth is allowed. This is the exponential premium principle, also called the entropic premium. It is finite when the required exponential moment exists (which is not the case for heavy-tailed claims). It is monotone, cash additive and convex, and it is at least as large as the expectation. Independence gives
\[
\mathbb E[e^{\gamma(X+Y)}]
=\mathbb E[e^{\gamma X}]\mathbb E[e^{\gamma Y}],
\quad\text{so}\quad
\pi(X+Y)=\pi(X)+\pi(Y).
\]
But it is not generally subadditive. For a bounded non-constant \(X\), the strict positivity of \(\mathbb V(e^{\gamma X})\) yields
\[
\mathbb E[e^{2\gamma X}]>\bigl(\mathbb E[e^{\gamma X}]\bigr)^2,
\quad\text{hence}\quad
\pi(2X)>2\pi(X).
\]
This also disproves positive homogeneity. The fixed-parameter domain \(\{X:\mathbb E[e^{\gamma X}]<\infty\}\) is not generally closed under addition: having a finite premium for each of two claims need not give a finite premium for their sum. The bounded example above avoids this domain issue.

All these principles are law invariant and dominate the expectation for non-negative claims in their respective domains. Yet each has a limitation for the intended pricing task: no risk margin, no distinction between equal-mean claims, failure of monotonicity, failure of scaling or aggregation properties, or restrictive integrability.
There is no contradiction here. Different formulas encode different economic objectives. The next question is how much of a real premium should be determined by a stand-alone mathematical principle in the first place.

title: Insurance pricing and risk measures
text:
4.2 A detour through pricing practice

4.2.1 A premium is assembled from several ingredients
In practice, insurers combine statistical estimates, expense allowances, reinsurance costs, capital costs and commercial adjustments. The resulting premium rarely follows one universal formula \(\pi(X)\) applied mechanically to every individual contract.
A simple illustrative calculation starts from expected annual claims \(m\). Suppose there are fixed expenses \(e\), proportional expenses equal to a fraction \(a\in[0,1)\) of the premium, and a monetary allowance \(k\) for bearing risk, including the cost of the contract’s contribution to the insurer’s regulatory capital requirement. Balancing the amounts gives
\[
p=m+e+ap+k,
\quad\text{hence}\quad
p=\frac{m+e+k}{1-a}.
\]
For \(m=300\), \(e=40\), \(k=20\), and \(a=0.20\), the indicated premium is \(450\). This example is before any separate taxes and assumes no investment income. The allowance \(k\) includes the cost of maintaining the capital associated with the contract over the pricing period, rather than charging the policyholder the whole amount of that capital.
The estimates and allowances are then adjusted to reflect the contract, the insurer’s experience and commercial considerations. The important point is that the final premium combines several ingredients, some of which depend on the insurer’s portfolio as a whole.


4.2.2 The risk belongs to the portfolio
Suppose the insurer already faces an aggregate loss \(S\) and is considering a new contract with loss \(X\). The additional risk depends on the joint distribution of \((S,X)\), not only on the distribution of \(X\). Even for variance,
\[
\mathbb V(S+X)-\mathbb V(S)=\mathbb V(X)+2\operatorname{Cov}(S,X).
\]
Two contracts with identical stand-alone distributions may make very different contributions to the insurer’s risk. A household policy that shares a flood exposure with thousands of existing policies is not equivalent, for the insurer, to an otherwise similar policy in a different region.
If \(K(S)\) denotes a portfolio capital requirement, an incremental approach may examine
\[
K(S+X)-K(S).
\]
A pricing allowance might remunerate this additional capital over the contract period. Other approaches allocate the total capital among contracts or business lines. The allocation problem is separate from the definition of the total requirement.
This is why risk measures at the portfolio level become central. We now want a numerical assessment of the insurer’s aggregate loss, for risk limits, capital allocation or solvency assessment. This is a general risk-management question, relevant in banking as well as insurance.


4.2.3 Loss measures and capital requirements
In what follows, we also allow for gains, so \(X\) may take negative values. We retain the loss convention: larger values of \(X\) are worse. All amounts are expressed at a common horizon and in a common monetary unit.
A risk measure \(\rho(X)\) gives a monetary assessment of the portfolio loss. It can be used to set risk limits, allocate capital or assess the resources needed to withstand adverse outcomes. These questions concern the insurer’s overall financial position, including both its assets and its liabilities.
For a simple balance-sheet interpretation, let \(S\) be total claims and \(P\) the deterministic premium income available to pay them. Ignore expenses, investment income and other existing resources. The insurer’s net loss before any additional capital is \(S-P\). If \(\rho\) is cash additive, then
\[
\rho(S-P)=\rho(S)-P.
\]
Adding deterministic capital \(K\geq0\) reduces the remaining net loss to \(S-P-K\). Suppose that the risk criterion requires this position to have a non-positive risk measure. Cash additivity gives
\[
\rho(S-P-K)=\rho(S)-P-K,
\]
so the criterion is satisfied exactly when \(P+K\geq\rho(S)\). The smallest non-negative capital amount needed is therefore
\[
K=\bigl(\rho(S-P)\bigr)_+
=\bigl(\rho(S)-P\bigr)_+.
\]
With pure-premium income \(P=\mathbb E[S]\), this becomes \(K=(\rho(S)-\mathbb E[S])_+\). Thus a monetary assessment of gross claims and the capital needed in addition to premium income are different amounts. The contract premium is a third quantity: it may include an allowance for the cost of maintaining capital, without charging policyholders the entire capital amount.
In a more complete model, we would work with the insurer’s net financial position and account consistently for all assets, liabilities and cash flows. The simple formula above explains the distinction. It is not a regulatory capital formula.
Risk measures also enter regulatory capital calculations.
Article 101 of Solvency II (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2009) calibrates the Solvency Capital Requirement to a 99.5% Value-at-Risk standard over one year, in relation to basic own funds. It covers the undertaking’s risks, rather than defining the premium of each insurance policy. The standard formula or an approved internal model implements this framework. The formula for the quantile of an individual claim is not, by itself, a regulatory capital calculation.

title: Insurance pricing and risk measures
text:
4.3 Value-at-Risk: a loss threshold

4.3.1 Definition
Let \(X\) be an almost surely finite real-valued loss, with cumulative distribution function
\[
F_X(x)=\mathbb P(X\leq x).
\]
For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)
=F_X^{-1}(\alpha)
=\inf\{x\in\mathbb R \mid F_X(x)\geq\alpha\}.
\]
No moment assumption is needed. This quantile is finite for every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Right-continuity of \(F_X\) ensures that the infimum is attained: VaR is the smallest threshold whose cumulative probability is at least \(\alpha\).
The quantile satisfies
\[
F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)-)\leq\alpha
\leq F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)),
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\mathbb P(X<\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))\leq\alpha
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathbb P(X\leq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))\geq\alpha.
\]
In particular, \(\mathbb P(X>\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))\leq1-\alpha\). These inequalities are essential when there are atoms, but they do not uniquely characterise the lower quantile when the CDF has a plateau at level \(\alpha\). The equation \(F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))=\alpha\) does not hold in general.








Figure 4.1: Three cases for the lower quantile: a standard normal loss at level 0.9; masses 0.6 at zero and 0.4 at two, at level 0.8; and an equal mixture of uniform distributions on (0,1) and (2,3), at level 0.5.





As Figure 4.1 illustrates, for a continuous and strictly increasing CDF, the quantile is the unique solution of \(F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))=\alpha\). At a jump, the horizontal level \(\alpha\) can lie strictly between \(F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)-)\) and \(F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))\). On a plateau at height \(\alpha\), several values solve \(F_X(x)=\alpha\). Our definition selects the left endpoint. Thus continuity of the CDF alone does not ensure a unique solution to that equation.


4.3.2 Properties of Value-at-Risk

Proposition 4.1 (Basic properties) For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), Value-at-Risk is law invariant, monotone, cash additive and positively homogeneous. It is exact on constants. More explicitly,
\[
X\leq Y\text{ almost surely}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\leq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y),
\]
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X+c)=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)+c
\quad\text{for}\quad
c\in\mathbb R,
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(aX)=a\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)
\quad\text{for}\quad
a\geq0.
\]
Moreover, \(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\) is non-decreasing in \(\alpha\).


Proof. Law invariance follows from the definition. If \(X\leq Y\), then \(F_X(x)\geq F_Y(x)\) for every \(x\), so the first CDF reaches a given level no later than the second. For shifts, use \(F_{X+c}(x)=F_X(x-c)\). For \(a>0\), use \(F_{aX}(x)=F_X(x/a)\). The case \(a=0\) follows directly. A constant \(c\) has every quantile equal to \(c\). Finally, increasing the probability level can only move the first crossing to the right.

These are attractive properties. However, VaR need not dominate the expectation, and one major aggregation property is missing: VaR is not subadditive in general.


4.3.3 First counterexample: independent heavy-tailed losses
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be independent, with common density
\[
f(x)=\frac{\mathbf 1_{\{x\geq0\}}}{(1+x)^2}.
\]
For \(x\geq0\),
\[
\mathbb P(X>x)=\frac1{1+x}
\quad\text{and therefore}\quad
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}.
\]
For \(s\geq0\), conditioning on \(X\) and using independence gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(X+Y>s)
&=\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(Y>s-x)f_X(x)\,\mathrm dx\\
&=\int_0^s\frac{\mathrm dx}{(1+x)^2(1+s-x)}
+\int_s^\infty\frac{\mathrm dx}{(1+x)^2}\\
&=\frac1{1+s}
+\int_0^s\frac{\mathrm dx}{(1+x)^2(1+s-x)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
To evaluate the integral, use the partial fraction decomposition
\[
\frac1{(1+x)^2(1+s-x)}
=\frac1{(s+2)^2}\left(\frac1{1+x}+\frac1{1+s-x}\right)
+\frac1{s+2}\frac1{(1+x)^2}.
\]
It follows that
\[
\int_0^s\frac{\mathrm dx}{(1+x)^2(1+s-x)}
=\frac{2\log(1+s)}{(s+2)^2}
+\frac1{s+2}\left(1-\frac1{1+s}\right),
\]
and therefore
\[
\mathbb P(X+Y>s)
=\frac2{s+2}+\frac{2\log(1+s)}{(s+2)^2}.
\]
Evaluate this tail probability at the sum of the individual quantiles, \(2\alpha/(1-\alpha)\):
\[
\mathbb P\!\left(X+Y>\frac{2\alpha}{1-\alpha}\right)
=1-\alpha+\frac{(1-\alpha)^2}{2}\log\!\left(\frac{1+\alpha}{1-\alpha}\right)
>1-\alpha.
\]
The CDF of \(X+Y\) is continuous and increasing on \((0,+\infty)\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X+Y)
>\frac{2\alpha}{1-\alpha}
=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)+\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y).
\]
This works for every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), despite independence.
These particular losses have infinite expectation, since \(\int_0^{+\infty}(1+x)^{-1}\,\mathrm dx=+\infty\). The next example shows that the failure persists for bounded losses.


4.3.4 Second counterexample: credit insurance
Consider two credit insurance contracts with joint losses

Each contract pays nothing with probability \(96\%\). Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(X)=\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(Y)=0.
\]
Their sum is \(0\) with probability \(92\%\) and \(100\) with probability \(8\%\). Thus
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(X+Y)=100>0+0.
\]






NoteThe same marginal losses under independence



Keep the same marginal distributions as in the preceding credit-insurance example, but now assume that \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent: each pays \(100\) with probability \(0.04\) and \(0\) otherwise. Their joint distribution is

The individual 95% VaRs remain zero. For the sum,
\[
\mathbb P(X+Y\leq0)=0.9216<0.95

\]

\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(X+Y)=100

\]
The failure therefore occurs for bounded, independent claims as well.




4.3.5 What the threshold does not tell us
VaR answers a threshold question. It does not describe the severity of losses beyond that threshold. For example, if a loss is zero with probability \(96\%\) and equals \(M>0\) otherwise, its 95% VaR is zero for every value of \(M\).
In both credit examples, each individual probability of a positive payment lies below the 5% tail budget, whereas the probability that at least one contract pays exceeds it. A zero stand-alone VaR therefore does not mean that the contract is risk-free: it means that the chosen quantile lies at zero. The jump on aggregation shows why adding stand-alone VaRs can give a misleading assessment of portfolio risk. It should not be read as a general economic argument against pooling contracts.
The issue motivates a search for risk measures with better aggregation properties and a more explicit account of the upper tail.

title: Insurance pricing and risk measures
text:
4.4 Coherent risk measures
The influential paper by Artzner, Delbaen, Eber and Heath, Coherent Measures of Risk (Artzner et al. 1999), proposed four axioms for monetary risk measurement.1

Definition 4.1 (Coherent risk measure: loss convention) On a linear space of losses containing the constants, a finite-valued risk measure \(\rho\) is coherent if it satisfies:

Monotonicity: \(X\leq Y\) almost surely implies \(\rho(X)\leq\rho(Y)\).
Cash additivity: \(\rho(X+c)=\rho(X)+c\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R\).
Positive homogeneity: \(\rho(aX)=a\rho(X)\) for every \(a\geq0\).
Subadditivity: \(\rho(X+Y)\leq\rho(X)+\rho(Y)\).


These are very close to properties already considered for premium principles. Homogeneity gives \(\rho(0)=0\), cash additivity then gives \(\rho(c)=c\), and homogeneity together with subadditivity gives convexity. Law invariance is an additional property, not one of the four coherence axioms. A requirement such as \(\rho(X)\geq\mathbb E[X]\) is also not part of this definition.
The sign convention matters. If one uses future profit or wealth instead of losses, more money makes the position safer, and the signs in monotonicity and cash additivity change accordingly. Here we consistently work with losses.
VaR satisfies three of these four axioms but fails subadditivity. Can we retain a monetary interpretation while accounting for the losses in the upper tail?

title: Insurance pricing and risk measures
section: 4.5 Expected Shortfall: averaging the upper tail
text:
4.5 Expected Shortfall: averaging the upper tail

4.5.1 Why a conditional expectation is not the right starting definition
A tempting candidate is
\[
\mathbb E[X\mid X\geq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)].
\]
But why use \(\geq\) rather than \(>\)? If the distribution has an atom at the quantile, these conditions select different amounts of probability. Neither need select exactly \(1-\alpha\).
Take the individual credit loss above. At level \(95\%\), the quantile is zero, so
\[
\mathbb E[X\mid X\geq0]=4,
\quad\text{whereas}\quad
\mathbb E[X\mid X>0]=100.
\] The first averages the whole population of outcomes. The second averages only 4% of it. To average the worst 5%, we need all the positive losses and one further percentage point of zero losses. The correct answer will be \(80\).
There is another difficulty with the strict inequality: the event can have probability zero, for instance for a constant loss. We therefore begin with a definition that handles continuous and discrete distributions uniformly.


4.5.2 Definition by integrated quantiles
From now on, assume \(X\in L^1\), unless explicitly stated otherwise. For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define the Expected Shortfall at level \(\alpha\) by
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
=\frac1{1-\alpha}\int_{\alpha}^1\operatorname{VaR}_{u}(X)\,\mathrm du.
\]
The value at the endpoint \(u=1\) does not affect the integral. Since
\[
\int_0^1\left|F_X^{-1}(u)\right|\,\mathrm du=\mathbb E[|X|],
\]
ES is finite on \(L^1\). It is the average of the upper \(1-\alpha\) fraction of quantiles. In particular,
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)\geq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)\geq\mathbb E[X].
\]
The second inequality follows because the average of an increasing function over its upper interval is at least its average over the whole interval.


4.5.3 The stop-loss formula and the atom at the quantile

Proposition 4.2 (Two useful formulas) For \(X\in L^1\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\),
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
&=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\\
&\quad+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))_+].
\end{aligned}}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
&=\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{\{X>\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\}}]\\
&\quad+\frac{\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)}{1-\alpha}
\bigl(F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))-\alpha\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]


Proof. The generalised inverse is non-decreasing. Thus \(F_X^{-1}(u)\leq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\) for \(u<\alpha\), and \(F_X^{-1}(u)\geq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\) for \(u>\alpha\). To justify the quantile representation, let \(U\) be uniform on \((0,1)\), on an auxiliary space if necessary. The equivalence \(F_X^{-1}(u)\leq x\Longleftrightarrow u\leq F_X(x)\) for \(u\in(0,1)\) gives \(\mathbb P(F_X^{-1}(U)\leq x)=F_X(x)\). Thus \(F_X^{-1}(U)\) has the same distribution as \(X\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))_+]
&=\int_0^1\bigl(F_X^{-1}(u)-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\bigr)_+\,\mathrm du\\
&=\int_{\alpha}^1\bigl(F_X^{-1}(u)-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\bigr)\,\mathrm du\\
&=(1-\alpha)\bigl(\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Rearranging proves the first formula. For the second, expand
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))_+]
&=\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{\{X>\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\}}]\\
&\quad-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\mathbb P(X>\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))
\end{aligned}
\]
and use \(\mathbb P(X>\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))=1-F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))\).

The expectation \(\mathbb E[(X-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))_+]\) is a stop-loss premium, or the undiscounted expected payoff of a call on \(X\) with strike \(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\). Thus ES equals the VaR threshold plus the expected excess loss above that threshold, divided by \(1-\alpha\).
The second formula tells us precisely how to treat atoms. We include every outcome with \(X>\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\), whose total probability is \(1-F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))\). We then add probability mass \(F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))-\alpha\) from the outcomes with \(X=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\). There is enough probability mass at the threshold because
\[
0\leq F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))-\alpha
\leq\mathbb P(X=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)).
\]
If the CDF is continuous at \(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\), then \(F_X(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))=\alpha\) and there is no atom at the threshold. In that case,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
&=\mathbb E[X\mid X>\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)]\\
&=\mathbb E[X\mid X\geq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)].
\end{aligned}
\]
Without that condition, the atom correction must be retained.
For the original credit example with mutually exclusive positive payments,
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{0.95}(X)=\operatorname{ES}_{0.95}(Y)
=\frac{0.04\times100}{0.05}=80,
\]
whereas
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(X+Y)=100
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{ES}_{0.95}(X+Y)=100.
\]
The aggregation inequality now holds: \(100\leq80+80\).
In the independent variant, the individual ES values are still \(80\). The sum pays \(200\) with probability \(0.0016\) and \(100\) with probability \(0.0768\). Its worst 5% consists of all the outcomes with loss \(200\) and a probability mass of \(0.05-0.0016=0.0484\) taken from the outcomes with loss \(100\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{0.95}(X+Y)
=\frac{0.0016\times200+0.0484\times100}{0.05}
=103.2\leq80+80.
\]
The fraction of the atom included at the quantile matters. Conditioning on every outcome with loss at least \(100\) would average over 7.84% of the distribution, rather than the required 5%, and would give a different number. ES selects a prescribed upper-tail probability mass, including only the necessary fraction of a boundary atom.

title: Insurance pricing and risk measures
section: 4.6 ES as a worst-case stress test
text:
4.6 ES as a worst-case stress test

4.6.1 A uniform representation of the loss
Work on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), where \(\mathcal F\) is the \(\sigma\)-algebra of events. We assume that the space is rich enough to support an auxiliary uniform random variable independent of the losses under consideration. This can always be achieved by enlarging the probability space, without changing the joint distribution of those losses. It is a technical detail with no practical effect on the calculations below.
For a given loss \(X\), we can then construct a uniform random variable \(U\) on \((0,1)\) such that
\[
X=F_X^{-1}(U)\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]






NoteConstructing the uniform random variable



If \(V\) is uniform on \((0,1)\) and independent of \(X\), set
\[
U=F_X(X-)+V\bigl(F_X(X)-F_X(X-)\bigr),
\]
where \(F_X(x-)=\mathbb P(X<x)\). Then \(U\) is uniform and \(F_X^{-1}(U)=X\) almost surely. At an atom of the distribution, \(V\) spreads its probability mass uniformly across the corresponding jump of the CDF. If the CDF is continuous, the formula reduces to \(U=F_X(X)\).
The constructed \(U\) is generally dependent on \(X\). This dependence gives the almost sure identity above, rather than merely equality in distribution.



Proposition 4.3 (Worst-event representation) On such a space, for every \(X\in L^1\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\),
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
=\frac1{1-\alpha}\sup_{\substack{B\in\mathcal F\\\mathbb P(B)=1-\alpha}}
\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_B].}
\]
The supremum is attained.


Proof. Choose \(U\) uniform on \((0,1)\) such that \(X=F_X^{-1}(U)\) almost surely. Then \(\mathbb P(U>\alpha)=1-\alpha\) and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{\{U>\alpha\}}]
&=\mathbb E[F_X^{-1}(U)\mathbf 1_{\{U>\alpha\}}]\\
&=\int_{\alpha}^1F_X^{-1}(u)\,\mathrm du\\
&=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X).
\end{aligned}
\]
Let \(B\in\mathcal F\) satisfy \(\mathbb P(B)=1-\alpha\). By monotonicity of \(F_X^{-1}\),
\[
\bigl(X-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\bigr)
\bigl(\mathbf 1_{\{U>\alpha\}}-\mathbf 1_B\bigr)\geq0
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
Indeed, on \(\{U>\alpha\}\), both factors are non-negative. On \(\{U\leq\alpha\}\), both are non-positive. Taking expectations and using \(\mathbb P(U>\alpha)=\mathbb P(B)\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{\{U>\alpha\}}]-\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_B]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\bigl(X-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\bigr)
\bigl(\mathbf 1_{\{U>\alpha\}}-\mathbf 1_B\bigr)\right]\\
&\geq0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The event \(\{U>\alpha\}\) therefore attains the supremum, with the claimed value.



4.6.2 Interpretation and coherence
Since every admissible \(B\) has probability \(1-\alpha\), the representation can also be written
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
=\sup_{\mathbb P(B)=1-\alpha}\mathbb E[X\mid B].
\] We consider every event with the prescribed probability \(1-\alpha\) and retain the largest conditional mean loss. The worst event selects the largest losses, splitting the quantile atom if necessary. Thus “worst-case” refers to the worst average over a fixed probability mass, not to the largest possible individual loss. The calculation is made under the specified loss distribution: it does not by itself protect against an incorrectly modelled tail. This is a mathematical stress-test interpretation. Practical stress scenarios are often chosen in other ways and need not come with a reliable probability.
It also makes subadditivity transparent. For any \(B\in\mathcal F\) with \(\mathbb P(B)=1-\alpha\), first separate the two expectations, then bound each by its supremum:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X+Y)\mathbf 1_B]
&=\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_B]+\mathbb E[Y\mathbf 1_B]\\
&\leq\sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F\\\mathbb P(A)=1-\alpha}}\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_A]
+\sup_{\substack{C\in\mathcal F\\\mathbb P(C)=1-\alpha}}\mathbb E[Y\mathbf 1_C]\\
&=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
+(1-\alpha)\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(Y).
\end{aligned}
\]
The last equality follows from the worst-event representation applied separately to \(X\) and \(Y\). Taking the supremum over \(B\) on the left and using the same representation for \(X+Y\) gives
\[
(1-\alpha)\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X+Y)
\leq(1-\alpha)\bigl(\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)+\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(Y)\bigr).
\]
Dividing by \(1-\alpha\) proves
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X+Y)
\leq\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)+\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(Y).
\]
The worst event for the sum need not be the worst event for each component. That is exactly why the supremum of the sum is at most the sum of the suprema.
Monotonicity, cash additivity and positive homogeneity follow from the same representation, or directly from the quantile definition. Thus ES is a law-invariant coherent risk measure on \(L^1\).

title: Insurance pricing and risk measures
section: 4.7 ES as a minimum: the Rockafellar–Uryasev formula
text:
4.7 ES as a minimum: the Rockafellar–Uryasev formula
There is another representation, with a different interpretation and particularly useful computational consequences. Fix \(X\in L^1\), \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and define
\[
f(t)=t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]
\quad\text{for}\quad
t\in\mathbb R.
\]
We already know that \(f(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))=\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)\). The stronger statement is that this value is the minimum over every possible threshold.

Theorem 4.1 (Variational representation) For \(X\in L^1\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\),
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)\\
&\quad=\min_{t\in\mathbb R}\left\{t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]\right\},
\end{aligned}}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\in
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{t\in\mathbb R}f(t).}
\]


Proof. Set \(t_0=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\). For any real \(t\) and every realisation of \(X\),
\[
(X-t)_+-(X-t_0)_+
=-\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathbf 1_{\{X>s\}}\,\mathrm ds.
\]
The integrand is bounded by one and the interval is finite, so Fubini’s theorem allows us to interchange expectation and integration:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-t)_+-(X-t_0)_+]
&=-\mathbb E\!\left[
\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathbf 1_{\{X>s\}}\,\mathrm ds
\right]\\
&=-\int_{t_0}^{t}
\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\{X>s\}}]\,\mathrm ds\\
&=-\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathbb P(X>s)\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the definition of \(f\), we therefore obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(t)-f(t_0)
&=t-t_0
+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-t)_+-(X-t_0)_+]\\
&=t-t_0
-\frac1{1-\alpha}\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathbb P(X>s)\,\mathrm ds\\
&=\frac1{1-\alpha}\int_{t_0}^{t}(1-\alpha)\,\mathrm ds
-\frac1{1-\alpha}\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathbb P(X>s)\,\mathrm ds\\
&=\frac1{1-\alpha}\int_{t_0}^{t}
\bigl(1-\alpha-\mathbb P(X>s)\bigr)\,\mathrm ds\\
&=\frac1{1-\alpha}\int_{t_0}^{t}
\bigl(F_X(s)-\alpha\bigr)\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(t\geq t_0\), then \(F_X(s)\geq\alpha\) for \(s\geq t_0\), and the integral is non-negative. If \(t<t_0\), then \(F_X(s)<\alpha\) for \(s<t_0\), but the orientation of the integral is reversed, so it is again non-negative. Therefore \(f(t)\geq f(t_0)\) for every \(t\). The stop-loss formula identifies \(f(t_0)\) as ES.

No density or differentiability of the CDF has been assumed. The proof covers both atoms and plateaux.

4.7.1 A minimum value and a minimising threshold
The two boxes describe different objects: ES is the minimum value, whereas VaR is a minimising argument. The minimiser need not be unique. In fact,
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{t\in\mathbb R}f(t)
=\{t\in\mathbb R:F_X(t-)\leq\alpha\leq F_X(t)\}.
\]
For each realisation of \(X\), the function \(t\mapsto(X-t)_+\) is convex. Taking expectations, multiplying by the positive constant \(1/(1-\alpha)\) and adding \(t\) preserves convexity, so \(f\) is convex. Its one-sided derivatives are
\[
f'_-(t)=\frac{F_X(t-)-\alpha}{1-\alpha}
\quad\text{and}\quad
f'_+(t)=\frac{F_X(t)-\alpha}{1-\alpha}.
\]
The minimum condition is \(f'_-(t)\leq0\leq f'_+(t)\). If the CDF has a plateau at height \(\alpha\), the corresponding closed interval consists of minimisers, whereas our VaR convention selects its left endpoint. Its right endpoint is included even if the CDF jumps there: the condition uses \(F_X(t-)\) as well as \(F_X(t)\).
This should recall the least-squares characterisation from the previous chapter. For \(X\in L^2\),
\[
\mathbb V(X)=\min_{t\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E[(X-t)^2]
\quad\text{and}\quad
\{\mathbb E[X]\}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{t\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E[(X-t)^2],
\]
where the minimiser is unique. The parallel is between an optimal value and an optimal location:








Objective
Minimum value
Minimising location




\(\mathbb E[(X-t)^2]\)
\(\mathbb V(X)\)
\(\mathbb E[X]\), uniquely


\(t+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]\)
\(\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)\)
\(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\), possibly among others



This analogy concerns optimisation characterisations. It does not identify ES with a dispersion measure. In particular, ES is cash additive, whereas variance is unchanged by a deterministic shift.


4.7.2 A second proof of subadditivity
Use the minimum representation with threshold \(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)+\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y)\). This gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X+Y)
&\leq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)+\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y)\\
&\quad+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E\!\left[
\bigl(X+Y-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y)\bigr)_+\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
The inequality \((a+b)_+\leq a_++b_+\) implies
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E\!\left[\bigl(X+Y-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y)\bigr)_+\right]\\
&\qquad\leq\mathbb E[(X-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))_+]
+\mathbb E[(Y-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y))_+].
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining these inequalities and applying the stop-loss formula to \(X\) and \(Y\) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X+Y)
&\leq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)
+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))_+]\\
&\quad+\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y)
+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(Y-\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y))_+]\\
&=\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)+\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(Y).
\end{aligned}
\]
For further perspectives, see Embrechts and Wang (2015). Their seven proofs of the subadditivity of Expected Shortfall reveal different structures behind the same inequality.

title: Insurance pricing and risk measures
section: 4.8 Why minimising ES is computationally convenient
text:
4.8 Why minimising ES is computationally convenient
The minimum representation is not only a proof device. Suppose a decision \(a\in\mathcal A\) determines a loss \(X_a\). The decision could represent portfolio holdings, reinsurance protection or exposure limits. We want to minimise \(\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X_a)\).
Formally, assuming the minima are attained,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{a\in\mathcal A}\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X_a)
&=\min_{a\in\mathcal A}\min_{t\in\mathbb R}
\left\{t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X_a-t)_+]\right\}\\
&=\min_{\substack{a\in\mathcal A\\t\in\mathbb R}}
\left\{t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X_a-t)_+]\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Without attainment, the same equality holds with infima. The central observation is simple: a minimum of minima is a joint minimum. We introduce the threshold as one additional decision variable and optimise it together with the portfolio. There is no need to recompute a quantile by a separate inner procedure for every trial portfolio.
For a finite collection of loss scenarios \(x_j(a)\) with probabilities \(p_j>0\) satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^N p_j=1\), the objective becomes
\[
\min_{\substack{a\in\mathcal A\\t\in\mathbb R}}\left\{t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\sum_{j=1}^N p_j(x_j(a)-t)_+\right\}.
\]
Introduce variables \(z_1,\ldots,z_N\) for the excess losses. The problem is equivalent to
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{minimise}\quad
&t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\sum_{j=1}^N p_jz_j\\
\text{over}\quad
&a\in\mathcal A,\quad t\in\mathbb R,\quad z_1,\ldots,z_N\in\mathbb R\\
\text{subject to}\quad
&z_j\geq x_j(a)-t\quad\text{and}\quad z_j\geq0,
\quad\text{for}\quad j=1,\ldots,N.
\end{aligned}
\]
At an optimum, each \(z_j\) equals \((x_j(a)-t)_+\), because its coefficient in the objective is positive. If the scenario losses are affine in the decisions and the feasible set is described by linear constraints, this is a linear programme. If the losses are convex and the feasible set is convex, the joint problem remains convex. The treatment of atoms and fractional tail probabilities is automatic.
This is the practical force of the Rockafellar–Uryasev approach (Rockafellar and Uryasev 2000, 2002).
The reformulation does not make every insurance decision easy: integer constraints, non-convex contract structures or difficult loss models may remain. Nor does it remove the statistical difficulty of estimating rare losses. It does, however, give ES a particularly convenient optimisation structure once a tractable scenario model is available.
This is also why the distinction between VaR and ES matters beyond insurance. The Basel market-risk framework uses a 97.5% ES standard within its internal models approach (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision 2020), with further requirements on stress calibration and liquidity horizons. This differs from Solvency II’s one-year 99.5% VaR calibration: the measures, horizons and regulatory constructions should not be conflated.

title: Insurance pricing and risk measures
text:
Key takeaways







A premium principle assigns a price to a claim. Natural requirements include monotonicity, cash additivity, positive homogeneity, subadditivity and convexity; none of the classical principles studied here satisfies them all while including a genuine risk loading.
The standard deviation and variance principles can violate monotonicity: they may charge more for a claim than for a certain payment that dominates it. The exponential principle is monotone and convex, but neither positively homogeneous nor subadditive.
An actual premium combines expected claims, expenses and an allowance for risk and capital. The risk a contract adds depends on the portfolio it joins, through its dependence with the existing risks.
Value-at-Risk is the lower quantile \(F_X^{-1}(\alpha)\). It is monotone, cash additive and positively homogeneous, but not subadditive, even for independent or bounded losses, and it ignores the size of losses beyond the threshold.
Expected Shortfall averages the quantiles above level \(\alpha\). It equals \(\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(X)+\mathbb E[(X-\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(X))_+]/(1-\alpha)\), includes only the required fraction of an atom at the quantile, and is a coherent risk measure.
ES is the worst average loss over events of probability \(1-\alpha\), a representation that makes subadditivity transparent.
ES is the minimum value of \(t+\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]/(1-\alpha)\), and VaR is a minimiser (Rockafellar–Uryasev). Minimising ES over a finite set of scenarios therefore becomes a linear or convex programme.

title: Insurance pricing and risk measures
text:
Footnotes


The subject was closely connected to practical risk management. During an informal discussion, Jean-Marc Eber, one of the paper’s authors, told me about its origins. He was at Société Générale in Paris at the time of the work and had encountered failures of VaR subadditivity in actual banking data. Aggregation problems were therefore not merely a mathematical curiosity: controls applied to individual positions could give a misleading impression of the risk of their sum.↩︎

title: Microeconomics of insurance
text:
Before studying the demand for insurance, we need a language for describing preferences under risk: how does an individual compare a sure wealth level with a risky one, or choose between two risky wealth levels? We begin with these preferences and then introduce a mathematical representation that will allow us to study risk aversion and insurance decisions.


Fix a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) and an interval \(\mathcal I\subseteq\mathbb R\) with non-empty interior. We consider an agent’s preferences over random total wealth levels taking values in \(\mathcal I\). The interval may be unbounded: the main examples will be \(\mathbb R\), \((0,\infty)\) and \([0,\infty)\).
The agent weakly prefers a wealth \(Y\) to a wealth \(X\) if they either strictly prefer \(Y\) or are indifferent between the two. The word weakly includes indifference.
We assume that these preferences admit an expected-utility representation: there exists a function \(u:\mathcal I\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[
X\precsim_u Y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathbb E[u(X)]\leq\mathbb E[u(Y)].
\]
The function \(u\) is a utility function of wealth. It represents the agent’s preferences by assigning to each random wealth its expected utility. The notation \(X\precsim_u Y\) expresses weak preference for \(Y\) over \(X\), with the subscript indicating the representing utility. Strict preference and indifference are denoted by \(\prec_u\) and \(\sim_u\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
X\prec_u Y
&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbb E[u(X)]<\mathbb E[u(Y)]
&&\text{(strict preference)},\\
X\sim_u Y
&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbb E[u(X)]=\mathbb E[u(Y)]
&&\text{(indifference)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the expected-utility framework of von Neumann and Morgenstern, whose book Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944) introduced the framework, with an axiomatic derivation of numerical utility added in the second edition (Neumann and Morgenstern 1947). The point is not that individuals literally write down a utility function before making a decision. Rather, the function provides a mathematical representation of their preferences under risk.






NoteUtility is not unique



If \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), then \(u\) and \(\widetilde u=\alpha u+\beta\) represent exactly the same preferences. Any economically meaningful quantity derived from utility should therefore be invariant under increasing affine transformations. The affine restriction matters: an arbitrary increasing transformation need not preserve expected-utility comparisons.








ImportantStanding assumptions



The following conventions apply throughout the chapter unless stated otherwise.
Utility functions. Every utility function is continuous on its interval of definition \(\mathcal I\) and belongs to \(C^2(\mathcal I^\circ)\), with, on \(\mathcal I^\circ\),
\[
u'>0
\quad\text{and}\quad
u''\leq 0.
\]
We shall state it explicitly when the stronger condition \(u''<0\) is required. Every random wealth to which utility is applied takes values in \(\mathcal I\) almost surely.
Integrability. We restrict attention to random variables for which all the expectations under consideration are well defined and finite. The precise integrability conditions depend jointly on the random variable and on the utility function.
Monotonicity. Increasing and decreasing mean strictly monotone. We use non-decreasing and non-increasing when equality is allowed.


The condition \(u'>0\) implies that more wealth is preferred to less. The condition \(u''\leq0\) says that the marginal utility of wealth is non-increasing: an additional euro matters no more (and typically less) at a higher wealth level. If \(u''(x)=0\) for all \(x\), then \(u\) is affine and increasing (we often normalise it to \(u(x)=x\)), and the agent is said to be risk-neutral.
The geometric meaning of concavity is useful to keep in mind. For \(x_0,x_1\in\mathcal I\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\),
\[
u\bigl(\theta x_0+(1-\theta)x_1\bigr)
\geq
\theta u(x_0)+(1-\theta)u(x_1).
\]
The graph of a concave utility function therefore lies above every chord joining two points of the graph, as illustrated in Figure 2.1.








Figure 2.1: Concavity: the utility of average wealth exceeds the average utility. The dashed line is the chord.





In the figure, \(\bar x=\theta x_0+(1-\theta)x_1\) and \(\bar u=\theta u(x_0)+(1-\theta)u(x_1)\). Concavity gives \(u(\bar x)\geq\bar u\).
Concavity has an immediate interpretation under uncertainty.

Theorem 2.1 (Jensen’s inequality) Let \(u\) be concave on \(\mathcal I\) and let \(X\) be an integrable random variable with values in \(\mathcal I\) such that \(u(X)\) is integrable. Then
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
u\bigl(\mathbb E[X]\bigr).
\]
If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, meaning that \(X\) is not almost surely constant, the inequality is strict.

Under our concavity assumption, Jensen’s inequality always gives
\[
X\precsim_u\mathbb E[X].
\]
The agent weakly prefers a sure wealth level to any risky wealth with the same mean. When \(u\) is strictly concave, the above preference becomes strict for every non-degenerate random variable. The latter property is called risk aversion and we say that the agent is risk-averse. Some authors already speak of risk aversion for the weak preference; here we reserve the term for the strict one.
A simple classroom example illustrates risk aversion. Interpret the following amounts as additional payoffs added to initial wealth \(w\), and assume that all resulting wealth levels belong to \(\mathcal I\). Compare a sure €1 with a fair coin toss paying €0 or €2. At such small stakes, one may feel almost indifferent. Compare next a sure €10,000 with a fair gamble paying €0 or €20,000: the sure amount may now be much more attractive. Finally, consider a sure €250,000 versus a fair gamble paying €0 or €1,000,000. Choosing the sure amount, which most people in the classroom do, means accepting only half the expected payoff to avoid the uncertainty.
The last example raises a more informative question: what sure amount would make the individual indifferent to the gamble?
