Most people cannot specify their utility function – and, honestly, neither can I – but they can often give an intuitive answer to such a choice, or say whether they feel a proposed entry price makes a game worth playing. This motivates the concept of certainty equivalent and, for purchases of risky payoffs, that of indifference price.



The previous example suggests a natural way of attaching a monetary value to a risky prospect.

Definition 2.1 (Certainty equivalent) Let \(X\) take values in \(\mathcal I\) and assume that \(u(X)\) is integrable. The certainty equivalent of \(X\) for utility \(u\) is the unique sure wealth level \(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\in\mathcal I\) satisfying
\[
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr)
=
\mathbb E[u(X)].
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
u^{-1}\!\left(\mathbb E[u(X)]\right).
\]

The definition makes sense. Continuity and strict monotonicity of \(u\) imply that \(u(\mathcal I)\) is an interval and that \(u\) is a bijection from \(\mathcal I\) onto it. Since \(u(X)\) takes values in this interval, so does its finite mean \(\mathbb E[u(X)]\). Hence \(u^{-1}(\mathbb E[u(X)])\) is well defined and unique.
In French, the same object is called équivalent certain and often denoted \(ec_u(X)\).
The certainty equivalent is a monetary valuation of final wealth: it is the sure wealth level that makes the agent indifferent to the risky wealth \(X\).






NoteCertainty equivalents and indifference prices



When the random variable represents an incremental payoff rather than final wealth, it is often more natural to speak of an indifference price.
Suppose an agent has initial wealth \(w\in\mathcal I\) and considers buying a risky payoff \(Y\) for a price \(P\). We consider prices for which \(w+Y-P\in\mathcal I\) almost surely and \(u(w+Y-P)\) is integrable. The buyer’s indifference price \(P_u(w,Y)\) is defined, when it exists, by
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[u\bigl(w+Y-P_u(w,Y)\bigr)\right]
=
u(w).
\]
At a price \(P\), the agent compares \(\mathbb E[u(w+Y-P)]\) with \(u(w)\). Since utility is increasing, raising the price makes the purchase less attractive. If \(P_u(w,Y)\) solves the equation above, then the agent prefers buying at a lower admissible price, is indifferent at \(P_u(w,Y)\), and prefers not buying at a higher price. Thus \(P_u(w,Y)\) is the maximum acceptable price.
In general, \(P_u(w,Y)\) depends on initial wealth \(w\): it values the payoff \(Y\) in the context of the individual’s existing resources. By contrast, \(\operatorname{ce}_u(Y)\) treats \(Y\) itself as final wealth. Under CARA utility on \(\mathbb R\) (see below), translation invariance gives
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(w+Y-P)=w-P+\operatorname{ce}_u(Y),
\]
so the indifference condition reduces to
\[
P_u(w,Y)=\operatorname{ce}_u(Y).
\]



Proposition 2.1 (Certainty equivalent and the mean) Whenever the quantities are well defined,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\mathbb E[X].
\]
If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, then the inequality is strict.


Proof. By Jensen’s inequality,
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
u(\mathbb E[X]).
\]
By definition,
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr).
\]
Since \(u\) is increasing,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\mathbb E[X].
\]
Strict concavity and non-degeneracy give the strict version through the strict form of Jensen’s inequality.

The difference
\[
\Pi_u(X)
:=
\mathbb E[X]-\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\geq0
\]
is called the risk premium. It is the discount, relative to the expected value, associated with bearing the risk.






NoteThe St Petersburg paradox



The St Petersburg paradox illustrates why expected monetary value alone need not determine choices under risk. Nicolas Bernoulli posed the problem in his correspondence in 1713. Nowadays, the game would roughly proceed as follows: toss a fair coin; if it lands heads, the game ends and you receive €2. Otherwise, toss again: a head on the second toss pays €4. If the first two tosses are tails, continue, with €8 paid for a first head on the third toss, and so on. Each tail doubles the amount at stake, and the game ends at the first head.
Let \(N\) be the number of tosses until the first head and let \(Z_n=2^n\) be the payoff if the game ends on toss \(n\). A first head on toss \(n\) requires \(n-1\) tails followed by one head, so \(\mathbb P(N=n)=2^{-n}\). The game ends almost surely, but its payoff \(Z_N=2^N\) has infinite expectation (this example deliberately departs from our finite-expectation convention):
\[
\mathbb E[Z_N]
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}Z_n\mathbb P(N=n)
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^n2^{-n}
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1=+\infty.
\]
Every possible value of the stopping time contributes the same positive amount to the expectation. Yet the fact that the expected payoff is infinite does not make an arbitrarily large entry fee attractive.
Daniel Bernoulli’s celebrated 1738 response was to value wealth through a concave utility function rather than to maximise expected money directly (Bernoulli 1954, English translation of the 1738 Latin original). His central example was logarithmic utility. The episode is historically important because it makes the distinction between money and the utility of money explicit, long before the axiomatic formulation of expected utility by von Neumann and Morgenstern.





The certainty equivalent depends both on the distribution of the risk and on the agent’s utility function. For a small risk, these two effects separate particularly cleanly.
Let
\[
X_\varepsilon=\mu+\varepsilon Z,
\]
where
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
Thus \(\mu\) is the mean wealth and
\[
\mathbb V(X_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^2.
\]

Proposition 2.2 (Certainty equivalent of a small centred risk) Let \(\mu\in\mathcal I^\circ\), and let \(Z\) be bounded with
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
For sufficiently small \(|\varepsilon|\), we have
\[
[\mu-|\varepsilon|\|Z\|_\infty,\mu+|\varepsilon|\|Z\|_\infty]\subset\mathcal I,
\]
so \(\mu+\varepsilon Z\) takes values in \(\mathcal I\). Then, as \(\varepsilon\to0\),
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac12\frac{u''(\mu)}{u'(\mu)}\,\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]


Proof. Taylor’s formula with integral remainder gives
\[
u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=u(\mu)+\varepsilon Z u'(\mu)
+\varepsilon^2 Z^2\int_0^1(1-t)u''(\mu+t\varepsilon Z)\,\mathrm dt.
\]
Taking expectations and using \(\mathbb E[Z]=0\), we get
\[
\mathbb E[u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)]
=u(\mu)+\varepsilon^2\mathbb E\!\left[
Z^2\int_0^1(1-t)u''(\mu+t\varepsilon Z)\,\mathrm dt\right].
\]
Because \(Z\) is bounded, all arguments of \(u''\) stay in a fixed compact neighbourhood of \(\mu\) for small enough \(|\varepsilon|\). Continuity of \(u''\) and dominated convergence therefore give
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[Z^2\int_0^1(1-t)u''(\mu+t\varepsilon Z)\,\mathrm dt\right]
\longrightarrow \frac12u''(\mu)\mathbb E[Z^2]=\frac12u''(\mu).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)]
=u(\mu)+\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2+o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
u^{-1}\!\left(
u(\mu)
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right).
\]
A first-order expansion of \(u^{-1}\) at \(u(\mu)\) therefore yields
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac{1}{u'(\mu)}
\left(
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right),
\]
which is the stated result.

The expansion separates two ingredients. The amount of risk is represented by the variance \(\varepsilon^2\), while the local attitude towards risk is captured by the curvature ratio \(-u''(\mu)/u'(\mu)\) evaluated at the mean \(\mu\).
This motivates the fundamental definition.

Definition 2.2 (Risk aversion coefficients) The coefficient of absolute risk aversion associated with a utility function \(u\) is
\[
\gamma_u(x)
:=
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
\quad\text{for}\quad
x\in\mathcal I^\circ.
\]
For \(x\in\mathcal I^\circ\cap(0,\infty)\), the corresponding coefficient of relative risk aversion is
\[
\rho_u(x)
:=
x\,\gamma_u(x).
\]

The coefficient is classically associated with the work of Arrow and Pratt (Arrow 1971; Pratt 1964).
Because \(u\) is concave and \(u'>0\), \(\gamma_u(x)\geq0\). More importantly, \(\gamma_u\) is unchanged when \(u\) is replaced by \(\alpha u+\beta\) with \(\alpha>0\): it therefore depends on preferences, not on the arbitrary choice of a utility representation.
With this notation, Proposition 2.2 becomes
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
-
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2),
\]
or, equivalently,
\[
\Pi_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
Dropping the remainder gives the Arrow–Pratt approximation:
\[
\Pi_u(X)\approx\frac12\gamma_u(\mathbb E[X])\mathbb V(X).
\]
It is a local approximation for risks concentrated near their mean, not an exact formula for arbitrary risks (except in specific cases, see below).
The leading-order cost of a small risk is therefore half the product of a risk term, its variance, and a preference term, the coefficient of absolute risk aversion evaluated at the mean wealth \(\mu\).



A particularly tractable case is that of constant absolute risk aversion (CARA). Its traditional domain is \(\mathbb R\): the exponential and affine specifications below are defined for every real wealth level, including negative net wealth.

Proposition 2.3 (Characterisation of CARA utility) Suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\gamma
\]
for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), where \(\gamma\geq0\) is constant and \(u\) is defined on \(\mathbb R\). Then:

if \(\gamma=0\), then \(u\) is affine and the agent is risk-neutral;
if \(\gamma>0\), then, up to an increasing affine transformation,

\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}.
\]
Conversely, an increasing affine utility function has coefficient zero, and, for \(\gamma>0\), \(u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}\) has constant absolute risk aversion equal to \(\gamma\).


Proof. The equation \(\gamma_u(x)=\gamma\) is
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\gamma,
\]
or equivalently
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\gamma.
\]
Hence
\[
u'(x)
=
C e^{-\gamma x},
\] where \(C>0\).
If \(\gamma>0\), integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A-B e^{-\gamma x},
\] where \(B>0\), which is equivalent under an increasing affine transformation to \(-e^{-\gamma x}\).
If \(\gamma=0\), then \(u'\) is constant and \(u\) is affine.
The rest of the proof is straightforward verification.

CARA is a strong assumption for individuals: with a CARA utility function, the willingness to bear a fixed monetary risk does not depend on wealth. In particular, for
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\] where \(\gamma>0\), we have
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
-\frac1\gamma
\log\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma X}],
\]
whenever the expectation is finite, and
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X+c)
=
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)+c.
\]
This translation invariance is, however, one reason CARA specifications are common in models of firms or delegated decision-makers when one wants to analyse profit risk without modelling wealth effects explicitly.
For Gaussian risks the Arrow–Pratt approximation is not an approximation at all in the case of a CARA utility function.

Proposition 2.4 (CARA utility and Gaussian risk) Let \(u\) be defined on \(\mathbb R\) by
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\] where \(\gamma>0\), and let \(\mu\in\mathbb R\) and \(\sigma\geq0\). Set
\[
X=\mu+\sigma Z,
\] where \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\).
Then
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\sigma^2.
\]


Proof. The moment-generating function of a standard Gaussian (two proofs are given in the note below) is
\[
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]
=
e^{t^2/2},
\]
so we obtain
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
-e^{-\gamma\mu}
\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma\sigma Z}]
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\sigma^2
\right).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
-e^{-\gamma\operatorname{ce}_u(X)}
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\sigma^2
\right),
\]
and therefore
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\sigma^2.
\]







NoteTwo ways to compute the Gaussian moment-generating function





Let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and define
\[
M(t)
=
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}].
\]
We show that
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]
1. Completing the square. Using the Gaussian density,
\[
M(t)
=
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
\exp\!\left(
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\,\mathrm dz.
\]
Since
\[
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
=
-\frac{(z-t)^2}{2}
+
\frac{t^2}{2},
\]
we obtain
\[
M(t)
=
e^{t^2/2}
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
e^{-(z-t)^2/2}\,\mathrm dz
=
e^{t^2/2}.
\]
2. A differential equation. Differentiation under the integral sign is legitimate: for \(|t|\leq T\), the derivative of the integrand is dominated by \(|z|\exp(T|z|-z^2/2)\), which is integrable. Hence
\[
M'(t)
=
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R} z
\exp\!\left(
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\,\mathrm dz = \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R} \exp(tz)\left(z
\exp\!\left(-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\right)\,\mathrm dz .
\]
Integration by parts (the boundary terms vanish) then gives
\[
M'(t) = \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R} t \exp(tz) \exp\left(
-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\,\mathrm dz
=
tM(t).
\]
Together with \(M(0)=1\), this differential equation has the unique solution
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]






Absolute risk aversion need not be constant. An agent exhibits

DARA (decreasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u\) is decreasing with wealth;
IARA (increasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u\) is increasing with wealth.

For individual decision-making, DARA is often regarded as more plausible than CARA: as wealth increases, a fixed monetary gamble becomes less important relative to the agent’s resources. Several empirical studies find absolute risk aversion decreasing with wealth, but the evidence is not uniform and estimated risk attitudes vary substantially across people and elicitation methods. DARA is therefore best viewed as an economically useful benchmark rather than as a universal empirical law; see, for example, (Guiso and Paiella 2008) and the rather different insurance-choice evidence in (Cohen and Einav 2007).
A second classical family imposes constant relative rather than absolute risk aversion. Its traditional domain is \((0,\infty)\) for \(\rho\geq1\), and may include zero when \(0<\rho<1\), as specified below.

Proposition 2.5 (Characterisation of CRRA utility) Let the domain be \((0,\infty)\) and suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\] where \(\rho>0\).
Then, up to an increasing affine transformation,
\[
u(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho},
& \rho\neq1,\\[1.1ex]
\log x,
& \rho=1.
\end{cases}
\]
Conversely, these utility functions satisfy
\[
\rho_u(x)
=
x\gamma_u(x)
=
\rho,
\]
and therefore have constant relative risk aversion for \(x>0\).
For the normalised functions displayed above, the traditional domains are:

\([0,\infty)\) when \(0<\rho<1\), with the continuous extension \(u(0)=0\);
\((0,\infty)\) when \(\rho\geq1\), with \(\lim_{x\downarrow0}u(x)=-\infty\).

When \(0<\rho<1\), differentiability is required only for \(x>0\); the continuous extension at zero satisfies our standing assumptions on \([0,\infty)\).


Proof. The equation
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
gives
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\]
hence
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\frac{\rho}{x}.
\]
Integrating,
\[
u'(x)
=
C x^{-\rho},
\] where \(C>0\).
A second integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\frac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}
\]
when \(\rho\neq1\), and
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\log x
\]
when \(\rho=1\), with \(B>0\).
Increasing affine transformations remove the irrelevant constants.

An agent with CRRA utility exhibits decreasing absolute risk aversion because
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
decreases with wealth. It also imposes a very specific rate of decline, and hence a rigid link between risk attitudes at different wealth levels: doubling wealth halves absolute risk aversion. The logarithmic case \(\rho=1\) is the specification associated with Daniel Bernoulli’s classical discussion of the St Petersburg paradox.



People can often answer questions about certainty equivalents – what sure amount would make you indifferent to this lottery? – much more readily than they can specify an entire utility function. It is therefore useful to have a way of comparing the risk aversion and the certainty equivalent of two agents without assigning cardinal meaning to the vertical scales of their utility functions.
Consider one agent represented by utility function \(u\) and another represented by utility function \(v\). The key mathematical idea is that one agent is at least as risk-averse as the other precisely when their utility can be obtained from the other’s by applying an additional increasing concave transformation.

Proposition 2.6 (Comparison of risk aversion) Let \(u\) and \(v\) be utility functions satisfying our standing assumptions on the same interval \(\mathcal I\). Then the following statements are equivalent:

for every \(x\in\mathcal I^\circ\),
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x);
\]
there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) on \(v(\mathcal I)\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]


In words, the agent represented by \(u\) is at least as risk-averse as the agent represented by \(v\) exactly when \(u\) is an increasing concave transformation of \(v\).

Proof. Because \(v\) is increasing, it is invertible on its range. Note first that if \(u=g\circ v\) for some function \(g\) on \(v(\mathcal I)\), then necessarily \(g=u\circ v^{-1}\): the transformation in statement 2 is unique. It therefore suffices to study
\[
g
:=
u\circ v^{-1}.
\]
Then \(u=g\circ v\), and \(g\) is increasing because both \(u\) and \(v^{-1}\) are increasing. Differentiating the identity
\[
g(v(x))
=
u(x)
\]
gives
\[
g'(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{v'(x)}
>
0.
\]
Differentiating once more,
\[
g''(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\left(
\gamma_v(x)-\gamma_u(x)
\right).
\]
The factor
\[
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\]
is positive. Hence
\[
g''\leq0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gamma_u\geq\gamma_v.
\]
Since \(g\) is continuous on \(v(\mathcal I)\) and twice differentiable on its interior, \(g\) is concave exactly when \(g''\leq0\) on that interior. This proves both directions. The same computation shows that \(\gamma_u>\gamma_v\) on \(\mathcal I^\circ\) implies \(g''<0\), hence strict concavity of \(g\).

The comparison has an immediate implication for certainty equivalents.

Proposition 2.7 (Ordering of certainty equivalents) Suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x)
\]
for every \(x\in\mathcal I^\circ\). Then, for every random variable \(X\) for which the certainty equivalents are well defined,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]
If moreover \(\gamma_u(x)>\gamma_v(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal I^\circ\) and \(X\) is non-degenerate, the inequality is strict.

Thus, when the agent represented by \(u\) is at least as risk-averse as the agent represented by \(v\), they assign to every risky prospect a certainty equivalent no higher than the other agent’s.

Proof. By Proposition 2.6, there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]
Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
\mathbb E[g(v(X))]
\leq
g\bigl(\mathbb E[v(X)]\bigr).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent under \(v\),
\[
\mathbb E[v(X)]
=
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
g\!\left(
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr)
\right)
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
But
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr).
\]
Since \(u\) is increasing,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]
Under the strict assumption, \(g\) is strictly concave (see the proof of Proposition 2.6). Since \(v\) is increasing and \(X\) is non-degenerate, \(v(X)\) is non-degenerate, so Jensen’s inequality above is strict, and so is the conclusion.

title: Microeconomics of insurance
text:
Before studying the demand for insurance, we need a language for describing preferences under risk: how does an individual compare a sure wealth level with a risky one, or choose between two risky wealth levels? We begin with these preferences and then introduce a mathematical representation that will allow us to study risk aversion and insurance decisions.


Fix a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) and an interval \(\mathcal I\subseteq\mathbb R\) with non-empty interior. We consider an agent’s preferences over random total wealth levels taking values in \(\mathcal I\). The interval may be unbounded: the main examples will be \(\mathbb R\), \((0,\infty)\) and \([0,\infty)\).
The agent weakly prefers a wealth \(Y\) to a wealth \(X\) if they either strictly prefer \(Y\) or are indifferent between the two. The word weakly includes indifference.
We assume that these preferences admit an expected-utility representation: there exists a function \(u:\mathcal I\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[
X\precsim_u Y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathbb E[u(X)]\leq\mathbb E[u(Y)].
\]
The function \(u\) is a utility function of wealth. It represents the agent’s preferences by assigning to each random wealth its expected utility. The notation \(X\precsim_u Y\) expresses weak preference for \(Y\) over \(X\), with the subscript indicating the representing utility. Strict preference and indifference are denoted by \(\prec_u\) and \(\sim_u\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
X\prec_u Y
&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbb E[u(X)]<\mathbb E[u(Y)]
&&\text{(strict preference)},\\
X\sim_u Y
&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbb E[u(X)]=\mathbb E[u(Y)]
&&\text{(indifference)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the expected-utility framework of von Neumann and Morgenstern, whose book Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944) introduced the framework, with an axiomatic derivation of numerical utility added in the second edition (Neumann and Morgenstern 1947). The point is not that individuals literally write down a utility function before making a decision. Rather, the function provides a mathematical representation of their preferences under risk.






NoteUtility is not unique



If \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), then \(u\) and \(\widetilde u=\alpha u+\beta\) represent exactly the same preferences. Any economically meaningful quantity derived from utility should therefore be invariant under increasing affine transformations. The affine restriction matters: an arbitrary increasing transformation need not preserve expected-utility comparisons.








ImportantStanding assumptions



The following conventions apply throughout the chapter unless stated otherwise.
Utility functions. Every utility function is continuous on its interval of definition \(\mathcal I\) and belongs to \(C^2(\mathcal I^\circ)\), with, on \(\mathcal I^\circ\),
\[
u'>0
\quad\text{and}\quad
u''\leq 0.
\]
We shall state it explicitly when the stronger condition \(u''<0\) is required. Every random wealth to which utility is applied takes values in \(\mathcal I\) almost surely.
Integrability. We restrict attention to random variables for which all the expectations under consideration are well defined and finite. The precise integrability conditions depend jointly on the random variable and on the utility function.
Monotonicity. Increasing and decreasing mean strictly monotone. We use non-decreasing and non-increasing when equality is allowed.


The condition \(u'>0\) implies that more wealth is preferred to less. The condition \(u''\leq0\) says that the marginal utility of wealth is non-increasing: an additional euro matters no more (and typically less) at a higher wealth level. If \(u''(x)=0\) for all \(x\), then \(u\) is affine and increasing (we often normalise it to \(u(x)=x\)), and the agent is said to be risk-neutral.
The geometric meaning of concavity is useful to keep in mind. For \(x_0,x_1\in\mathcal I\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\),
\[
u\bigl(\theta x_0+(1-\theta)x_1\bigr)
\geq
\theta u(x_0)+(1-\theta)u(x_1).
\]
The graph of a concave utility function therefore lies above every chord joining two points of the graph, as illustrated in Figure 2.1.








Figure 2.1: Concavity: the utility of average wealth exceeds the average utility. The dashed line is the chord.





In the figure, \(\bar x=\theta x_0+(1-\theta)x_1\) and \(\bar u=\theta u(x_0)+(1-\theta)u(x_1)\). Concavity gives \(u(\bar x)\geq\bar u\).
Concavity has an immediate interpretation under uncertainty.

Theorem 2.1 (Jensen’s inequality) Let \(u\) be concave on \(\mathcal I\) and let \(X\) be an integrable random variable with values in \(\mathcal I\) such that \(u(X)\) is integrable. Then
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
u\bigl(\mathbb E[X]\bigr).
\]
If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, meaning that \(X\) is not almost surely constant, the inequality is strict.

Under our concavity assumption, Jensen’s inequality always gives
\[
X\precsim_u\mathbb E[X].
\]
The agent weakly prefers a sure wealth level to any risky wealth with the same mean. When \(u\) is strictly concave, the above preference becomes strict for every non-degenerate random variable. The latter property is called risk aversion and we say that the agent is risk-averse. Some authors already speak of risk aversion for the weak preference; here we reserve the term for the strict one.
A simple classroom example illustrates risk aversion. Interpret the following amounts as additional payoffs added to initial wealth \(w\), and assume that all resulting wealth levels belong to \(\mathcal I\). Compare a sure €1 with a fair coin toss paying €0 or €2. At such small stakes, one may feel almost indifferent. Compare next a sure €10,000 with a fair gamble paying €0 or €20,000: the sure amount may now be much more attractive. Finally, consider a sure €250,000 versus a fair gamble paying €0 or €1,000,000. Choosing the sure amount, which most people in the classroom do, means accepting only half the expected payoff to avoid the uncertainty.
The last example raises a more informative question: what sure amount would make the individual indifferent to the gamble? Most people cannot specify their utility function – and, honestly, neither can I – but they can often give an intuitive answer to such a choice, or say whether they feel a proposed entry price makes a game worth playing. This motivates the concept of certainty equivalent and, for purchases of risky payoffs, that of indifference price.



The previous example suggests a natural way of attaching a monetary value to a risky prospect.

Definition 2.1 (Certainty equivalent) Let \(X\) take values in \(\mathcal I\) and assume that \(u(X)\) is integrable. The certainty equivalent of \(X\) for utility \(u\) is the unique sure wealth level \(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\in\mathcal I\) satisfying
\[
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr)
=
\mathbb E[u(X)].
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
u^{-1}\!\left(\mathbb E[u(X)]\right).
\]

The definition makes sense. Continuity and strict monotonicity of \(u\) imply that \(u(\mathcal I)\) is an interval and that \(u\) is a bijection from \(\mathcal I\) onto it. Since \(u(X)\) takes values in this interval, so does its finite mean \(\mathbb E[u(X)]\). Hence \(u^{-1}(\mathbb E[u(X)])\) is well defined and unique.
In French, the same object is called équivalent certain and often denoted \(ec_u(X)\).
The certainty equivalent is a monetary valuation of final wealth: it is the sure wealth level that makes the agent indifferent to the risky wealth \(X\).






NoteCertainty equivalents and indifference prices



When the random variable represents an incremental payoff rather than final wealth, it is often more natural to speak of an indifference price.
Suppose an agent has initial wealth \(w\in\mathcal I\) and considers buying a risky payoff \(Y\) for a price \(P\). We consider prices for which \(w+Y-P\in\mathcal I\) almost surely and \(u(w+Y-P)\) is integrable. The buyer’s indifference price \(P_u(w,Y)\) is defined, when it exists, by
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[u\bigl(w+Y-P_u(w,Y)\bigr)\right]
=
u(w).
\]
At a price \(P\), the agent compares \(\mathbb E[u(w+Y-P)]\) with \(u(w)\). Since utility is increasing, raising the price makes the purchase less attractive. If \(P_u(w,Y)\) solves the equation above, then the agent prefers buying at a lower admissible price, is indifferent at \(P_u(w,Y)\), and prefers not buying at a higher price. Thus \(P_u(w,Y)\) is the maximum acceptable price.
In general, \(P_u(w,Y)\) depends on initial wealth \(w\): it values the payoff \(Y\) in the context of the individual’s existing resources. By contrast, \(\operatorname{ce}_u(Y)\) treats \(Y\) itself as final wealth. Under CARA utility on \(\mathbb R\) (see below), translation invariance gives
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(w+Y-P)=w-P+\operatorname{ce}_u(Y),
\]
so the indifference condition reduces to
\[
P_u(w,Y)=\operatorname{ce}_u(Y).
\]



Proposition 2.1 (Certainty equivalent and the mean) Whenever the quantities are well defined,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\mathbb E[X].
\]
If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, then the inequality is strict.


Proof. By Jensen’s inequality,
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
u(\mathbb E[X]).
\]
By definition,
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr).
\]
Since \(u\) is increasing,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\mathbb E[X].
\]
Strict concavity and non-degeneracy give the strict version through the strict form of Jensen’s inequality.

The difference
\[
\Pi_u(X)
:=
\mathbb E[X]-\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\geq0
\]
is called the risk premium. It is the discount, relative to the expected value, associated with bearing the risk.






NoteThe St Petersburg paradox



The St Petersburg paradox illustrates why expected monetary value alone need not determine choices under risk. Nicolas Bernoulli posed the problem in his correspondence in 1713. Nowadays, the game would roughly proceed as follows: toss a fair coin; if it lands heads, the game ends and you receive €2. Otherwise, toss again: a head on the second toss pays €4. If the first two tosses are tails, continue, with €8 paid for a first head on the third toss, and so on. Each tail doubles the amount at stake, and the game ends at the first head.
Let \(N\) be the number of tosses until the first head and let \(Z_n=2^n\) be the payoff if the game ends on toss \(n\). A first head on toss \(n\) requires \(n-1\) tails followed by one head, so \(\mathbb P(N=n)=2^{-n}\). The game ends almost surely, but its payoff \(Z_N=2^N\) has infinite expectation (this example deliberately departs from our finite-expectation convention):
\[
\mathbb E[Z_N]
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}Z_n\mathbb P(N=n)
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^n2^{-n}
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1=+\infty.
\]
Every possible value of the stopping time contributes the same positive amount to the expectation. Yet the fact that the expected payoff is infinite does not make an arbitrarily large entry fee attractive.
Daniel Bernoulli’s celebrated 1738 response was to value wealth through a concave utility function rather than to maximise expected money directly (Bernoulli 1954, English translation of the 1738 Latin original). His central example was logarithmic utility. The episode is historically important because it makes the distinction between money and the utility of money explicit, long before the axiomatic formulation of expected utility by von Neumann and Morgenstern.





The certainty equivalent depends both on the distribution of the risk and on the agent’s utility function. For a small risk, these two effects separate particularly cleanly.
Let
\[
X_\varepsilon=\mu+\varepsilon Z,
\]
where
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
Thus \(\mu\) is the mean wealth and
\[
\mathbb V(X_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^2.
\]

Proposition 2.2 (Certainty equivalent of a small centred risk) Let \(\mu\in\mathcal I^\circ\), and let \(Z\) be bounded with
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
For sufficiently small \(|\varepsilon|\), we have
\[
[\mu-|\varepsilon|\|Z\|_\infty,\mu+|\varepsilon|\|Z\|_\infty]\subset\mathcal I,
\]
so \(\mu+\varepsilon Z\) takes values in \(\mathcal I\). Then, as \(\varepsilon\to0\),
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac12\frac{u''(\mu)}{u'(\mu)}\,\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]


Proof. Taylor’s formula with integral remainder gives
\[
u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=u(\mu)+\varepsilon Z u'(\mu)
+\varepsilon^2 Z^2\int_0^1(1-t)u''(\mu+t\varepsilon Z)\,\mathrm dt.
\]
Taking expectations and using \(\mathbb E[Z]=0\), we get
\[
\mathbb E[u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)]
=u(\mu)+\varepsilon^2\mathbb E\!\left[
Z^2\int_0^1(1-t)u''(\mu+t\varepsilon Z)\,\mathrm dt\right].
\]
Because \(Z\) is bounded, all arguments of \(u''\) stay in a fixed compact neighbourhood of \(\mu\) for small enough \(|\varepsilon|\). Continuity of \(u''\) and dominated convergence therefore give
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[Z^2\int_0^1(1-t)u''(\mu+t\varepsilon Z)\,\mathrm dt\right]
\longrightarrow \frac12u''(\mu)\mathbb E[Z^2]=\frac12u''(\mu).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)]
=u(\mu)+\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2+o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
u^{-1}\!\left(
u(\mu)
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right).
\]
A first-order expansion of \(u^{-1}\) at \(u(\mu)\) therefore yields
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac{1}{u'(\mu)}
\left(
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right),
\]
which is the stated result.

The expansion separates two ingredients. The amount of risk is represented by the variance \(\varepsilon^2\), while the local attitude towards risk is captured by the curvature ratio \(-u''(\mu)/u'(\mu)\) evaluated at the mean \(\mu\).
This motivates the fundamental definition.

Definition 2.2 (Risk aversion coefficients) The coefficient of absolute risk aversion associated with a utility function \(u\) is
\[
\gamma_u(x)
:=
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
\quad\text{for}\quad
x\in\mathcal I^\circ.
\]
For \(x\in\mathcal I^\circ\cap(0,\infty)\), the corresponding coefficient of relative risk aversion is
\[
\rho_u(x)
:=
x\,\gamma_u(x).
\]

The coefficient is classically associated with the work of Arrow and Pratt (Arrow 1971; Pratt 1964).
Because \(u\) is concave and \(u'>0\), \(\gamma_u(x)\geq0\). More importantly, \(\gamma_u\) is unchanged when \(u\) is replaced by \(\alpha u+\beta\) with \(\alpha>0\): it therefore depends on preferences, not on the arbitrary choice of a utility representation.
With this notation, Proposition 2.2 becomes
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
-
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2),
\]
or, equivalently,
\[
\Pi_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
Dropping the remainder gives the Arrow–Pratt approximation:
\[
\Pi_u(X)\approx\frac12\gamma_u(\mathbb E[X])\mathbb V(X).
\]
It is a local approximation for risks concentrated near their mean, not an exact formula for arbitrary risks (except in specific cases, see below).
The leading-order cost of a small risk is therefore half the product of a risk term, its variance, and a preference term, the coefficient of absolute risk aversion evaluated at the mean wealth \(\mu\).



A particularly tractable case is that of constant absolute risk aversion (CARA). Its traditional domain is \(\mathbb R\): the exponential and affine specifications below are defined for every real wealth level, including negative net wealth.

Proposition 2.3 (Characterisation of CARA utility) Suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\gamma
\]
for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), where \(\gamma\geq0\) is constant and \(u\) is defined on \(\mathbb R\). Then:

if \(\gamma=0\), then \(u\) is affine and the agent is risk-neutral;
if \(\gamma>0\), then, up to an increasing affine transformation,

\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}.
\]
Conversely, an increasing affine utility function has coefficient zero, and, for \(\gamma>0\), \(u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}\) has constant absolute risk aversion equal to \(\gamma\).


Proof. The equation \(\gamma_u(x)=\gamma\) is
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\gamma,
\]
or equivalently
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\gamma.
\]
Hence
\[
u'(x)
=
C e^{-\gamma x},
\] where \(C>0\).
If \(\gamma>0\), integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A-B e^{-\gamma x},
\] where \(B>0\), which is equivalent under an increasing affine transformation to \(-e^{-\gamma x}\).
If \(\gamma=0\), then \(u'\) is constant and \(u\) is affine.
The rest of the proof is straightforward verification.

CARA is a strong assumption for individuals: with a CARA utility function, the willingness to bear a fixed monetary risk does not depend on wealth. In particular, for
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\] where \(\gamma>0\), we have
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
-\frac1\gamma
\log\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma X}],
\]
whenever the expectation is finite, and
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X+c)
=
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)+c.
\]
This translation invariance is, however, one reason CARA specifications are common in models of firms or delegated decision-makers when one wants to analyse profit risk without modelling wealth effects explicitly.
For Gaussian risks the Arrow–Pratt approximation is not an approximation at all in the case of a CARA utility function.

Proposition 2.4 (CARA utility and Gaussian risk) Let \(u\) be defined on \(\mathbb R\) by
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\] where \(\gamma>0\), and let \(\mu\in\mathbb R\) and \(\sigma\geq0\). Set
\[
X=\mu+\sigma Z,
\] where \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\).
Then
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\sigma^2.
\]


Proof. The moment-generating function of a standard Gaussian (two proofs are given in the note below) is
\[
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]
=
e^{t^2/2},
\]
so we obtain
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
-e^{-\gamma\mu}
\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma\sigma Z}]
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\sigma^2
\right).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
-e^{-\gamma\operatorname{ce}_u(X)}
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\sigma^2
\right),
\]
and therefore
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\sigma^2.
\]







NoteTwo ways to compute the Gaussian moment-generating function





Let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and define
\[
M(t)
=
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}].
\]
We show that
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]
1. Completing the square. Using the Gaussian density,
\[
M(t)
=
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
\exp\!\left(
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\,\mathrm dz.
\]
Since
\[
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
=
-\frac{(z-t)^2}{2}
+
\frac{t^2}{2},
\]
we obtain
\[
M(t)
=
e^{t^2/2}
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
e^{-(z-t)^2/2}\,\mathrm dz
=
e^{t^2/2}.
\]
2. A differential equation. Differentiation under the integral sign is legitimate: for \(|t|\leq T\), the derivative of the integrand is dominated by \(|z|\exp(T|z|-z^2/2)\), which is integrable. Hence
\[
M'(t)
=
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R} z
\exp\!\left(
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\,\mathrm dz = \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R} \exp(tz)\left(z
\exp\!\left(-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\right)\,\mathrm dz .
\]
Integration by parts (the boundary terms vanish) then gives
\[
M'(t) = \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R} t \exp(tz) \exp\left(
-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\,\mathrm dz
=
tM(t).
\]
Together with \(M(0)=1\), this differential equation has the unique solution
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]






Absolute risk aversion need not be constant. An agent exhibits

DARA (decreasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u\) is decreasing with wealth;
IARA (increasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u\) is increasing with wealth.

For individual decision-making, DARA is often regarded as more plausible than CARA: as wealth increases, a fixed monetary gamble becomes less important relative to the agent’s resources. Several empirical studies find absolute risk aversion decreasing with wealth, but the evidence is not uniform and estimated risk attitudes vary substantially across people and elicitation methods. DARA is therefore best viewed as an economically useful benchmark rather than as a universal empirical law; see, for example, (Guiso and Paiella 2008) and the rather different insurance-choice evidence in (Cohen and Einav 2007).
A second classical family imposes constant relative rather than absolute risk aversion. Its traditional domain is \((0,\infty)\) for \(\rho\geq1\), and may include zero when \(0<\rho<1\), as specified below.

Proposition 2.5 (Characterisation of CRRA utility) Let the domain be \((0,\infty)\) and suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\] where \(\rho>0\).
Then, up to an increasing affine transformation,
\[
u(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho},
& \rho\neq1,\\[1.1ex]
\log x,
& \rho=1.
\end{cases}
\]
Conversely, these utility functions satisfy
\[
\rho_u(x)
=
x\gamma_u(x)
=
\rho,
\]
and therefore have constant relative risk aversion for \(x>0\).
For the normalised functions displayed above, the traditional domains are:

\([0,\infty)\) when \(0<\rho<1\), with the continuous extension \(u(0)=0\);
\((0,\infty)\) when \(\rho\geq1\), with \(\lim_{x\downarrow0}u(x)=-\infty\).

When \(0<\rho<1\), differentiability is required only for \(x>0\); the continuous extension at zero satisfies our standing assumptions on \([0,\infty)\).


Proof. The equation
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
gives
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\]
hence
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\frac{\rho}{x}.
\]
Integrating,
\[
u'(x)
=
C x^{-\rho},
\] where \(C>0\).
A second integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\frac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}
\]
when \(\rho\neq1\), and
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\log x
\]
when \(\rho=1\), with \(B>0\).
Increasing affine transformations remove the irrelevant constants.

An agent with CRRA utility exhibits decreasing absolute risk aversion because
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
decreases with wealth. It also imposes a very specific rate of decline, and hence a rigid link between risk attitudes at different wealth levels: doubling wealth halves absolute risk aversion. The logarithmic case \(\rho=1\) is the specification associated with Daniel Bernoulli’s classical discussion of the St Petersburg paradox.



People can often answer questions about certainty equivalents – what sure amount would make you indifferent to this lottery? – much more readily than they can specify an entire utility function. It is therefore useful to have a way of comparing the risk aversion and the certainty equivalent of two agents without assigning cardinal meaning to the vertical scales of their utility functions.
Consider one agent represented by utility function \(u\) and another represented by utility function \(v\). The key mathematical idea is that one agent is at least as risk-averse as the other precisely when their utility can be obtained from the other’s by applying an additional increasing concave transformation.

Proposition 2.6 (Comparison of risk aversion) Let \(u\) and \(v\) be utility functions satisfying our standing assumptions on the same interval \(\mathcal I\). Then the following statements are equivalent:

for every \(x\in\mathcal I^\circ\),
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x);
\]
there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) on \(v(\mathcal I)\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]


In words, the agent represented by \(u\) is at least as risk-averse as the agent represented by \(v\) exactly when \(u\) is an increasing concave transformation of \(v\).

Proof. Because \(v\) is increasing, it is invertible on its range. Note first that if \(u=g\circ v\) for some function \(g\) on \(v(\mathcal I)\), then necessarily \(g=u\circ v^{-1}\): the transformation in statement 2 is unique. It therefore suffices to study
\[
g
:=
u\circ v^{-1}.
\]
Then \(u=g\circ v\), and \(g\) is increasing because both \(u\) and \(v^{-1}\) are increasing. Differentiating the identity
\[
g(v(x))
=
u(x)
\]
gives
\[
g'(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{v'(x)}
>
0.
\]
Differentiating once more,
\[
g''(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\left(
\gamma_v(x)-\gamma_u(x)
\right).
\]
The factor
\[
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\]
is positive. Hence
\[
g''\leq0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gamma_u\geq\gamma_v.
\]
Since \(g\) is continuous on \(v(\mathcal I)\) and twice differentiable on its interior, \(g\) is concave exactly when \(g''\leq0\) on that interior. This proves both directions. The same computation shows that \(\gamma_u>\gamma_v\) on \(\mathcal I^\circ\) implies \(g''<0\), hence strict concavity of \(g\).

The comparison has an immediate implication for certainty equivalents.

Proposition 2.7 (Ordering of certainty equivalents) Suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x)
\]
for every \(x\in\mathcal I^\circ\). Then, for every random variable \(X\) for which the certainty equivalents are well defined,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]
If moreover \(\gamma_u(x)>\gamma_v(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal I^\circ\) and \(X\) is non-degenerate, the inequality is strict.

Thus, when the agent represented by \(u\) is at least as risk-averse as the agent represented by \(v\), they assign to every risky prospect a certainty equivalent no higher than the other agent’s.

Proof. By Proposition 2.6, there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]
Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
\mathbb E[g(v(X))]
\leq
g\bigl(\mathbb E[v(X)]\bigr).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent under \(v\),
\[
\mathbb E[v(X)]
=
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
g\!\left(
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr)
\right)
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
But
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr).
\]
Since \(u\) is increasing,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]
Under the strict assumption, \(g\) is strictly concave (see the proof of Proposition 2.6). Since \(v\) is increasing and \(X\) is non-degenerate, \(v(X)\) is non-degenerate, so Jensen’s inequality above is strict, and so is the conclusion.

title: Microeconomics of insurance
text:
2.2 Demand for insurance
Assumptions for this part. From now on, \(\mathcal I=\mathbb R_+^*=(0,\infty)\): \(u\) is a utility function of strictly positive wealth, with \(u\in C^2((0,\infty))\), \(u'>0\) and \(u''\leq0\). We shall explicitly impose \(u''<0\) where needed.
Since \(u\) is increasing, the limit
\[
u(0):=\lim_{x\downarrow0}u(x)\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}
\]
exists. This is only boundary notation: the strict parameter inequalities in each model below ensure that final wealth never reaches zero.
We now study the demand for insurance. We begin with the maximum amount an individual is willing to pay to eliminate a random loss. This willingness to pay depends on initial wealth, preferences and the loss distribution; it can be studied without specifying how insurers set prices.
We then introduce a pricing rule: the premium equals \(\lambda\geq1\) times the expected reimbursement (the pure premium). The excess over the pure premium is the safety loading. Under this rule, we first ask how much proportional coverage the individual purchases, and then allow the indemnity function to be chosen freely, subject to reimbursement lying between zero and the loss. The question becomes: which shape of insurance contract maximises expected utility?

2.2.1 Full insurance against a binary loss
We start with a binary loss to make the calculations explicit. The underlying approach extends to more general loss distributions, under suitable integrability assumptions.
An individual has initial wealth \(w\), including an asset worth \(S\), with \(0<S<w\). Thus losing the entire asset still leaves strictly positive wealth \(w-S\). The asset is completely lost with probability \(p\in(0,1)\) and remains intact with probability \(1-p\). The loss is modelled by the random variable
\[
X=\begin{cases}
0,&\text{with probability }1-p,\\
S,&\text{with probability }p.
\end{cases}
\]
Without insurance, the final wealth is \(w-X\). Full insurance reimburses the entire loss in exchange for an insurance premium \(0\leq\pi<w\), leaving the sure wealth \(w-\pi\). The insurance premium is the price of the policy; it is distinct from the risk premium \(\Pi_u\), which measures the utility cost of uncertainty in monetary terms.
The individual weakly prefers purchasing full insurance precisely when
\[
u(w-\pi)\geq\mathbb E[u(w-X)]
=(1-p)u(w)+p\,u(w-S).
\]
To summarise, the parameter restrictions are \(p\in(0,1)\), \(0<S<w\) and \(0\leq\pi<w\). They ensure that both uninsured wealth \(w-X\geq w-S\) and insured wealth \(w-\pi\) are strictly positive.

Proposition 2.8 (Maximum premium for full insurance) The maximum premium the individual is willing to pay is
\[
\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)
=w-u^{-1}\!\left((1-p)u(w)+p\,u(w-S)\right)
=w-\operatorname{ce}_u(w-X).
\]
It satisfies
\[
pS\leq\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)<S.
\]
If \(u''<0\), the lower bound is strict: a risk-averse individual is willing to pay strictly more than the pure premium. Moreover, \(\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\) is increasing in \(p\) and in \(S\), holding the other variables fixed.


Proof. Because \(p\in(0,1)\) and \(u\) is increasing,
\[
u(w-S)<(1-p)u(w)+p\,u(w-S)<u(w).
\]
Continuity and strict monotonicity of \(u\) therefore give a unique \(\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\in(0,S)\) satisfying the indifference equation
\[
u\!\left(w-\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\right)
=(1-p)u(w)+p\,u(w-S).
\]
Applying \(u^{-1}\) gives the stated formula. Since expected utility under full insurance decreases with its price, the agent weakly prefers insurance exactly for admissible premiums \(\pi\leq\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\).
Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(w-X)\leq\mathbb E[w-X]=w-pS,
\]
hence \(\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\geq pS\). When \(u''<0\), Jensen’s inequality is strict because \(w-X\) is non-degenerate, and so is the bound.
Finally, recalling that
\[
(u^{-1})'(y)=\frac{1}{u'(u^{-1}(y))},
\]
we differentiate the explicit formula to obtain
\[
\frac{\partial\pi_{\max}}{\partial p}(p,S,w)
=\frac{u(w)-u(w-S)}{u'\!\left(w-\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\right)}>0,
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial\pi_{\max}}{\partial S}(p,S,w)
=\frac{p\,u'(w-S)}{u'\!\left(w-\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\right)}>0.
\]

The lower bound \(pS=\mathbb E[X]\) is the pure premium, or actuarially fair premium, for full insurance. Willingness to pay exceeds this amount by exactly the risk premium of uninsured wealth:
\[
\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)=\mathbb E[X]+\Pi_u(w-X).
\]


2.2.2 How does willingness to pay depend on wealth?
The effects of \(p\) and \(S\) are intuitive: a more likely loss or a more valuable asset makes full insurance more attractive. Asking the same question about wealth often divides the classroom. One intuition is that a wealthier individual can more easily replace the asset and therefore has less need for insurance. Another is that paying a given premium is less burdensome at higher wealth. Neither intuition alone answers the question: both the loss and the premium must be evaluated through the same utility function.
There is no general direction for the wealth effect unless additional assumptions are made. The answer depends in fact on how absolute risk aversion changes with wealth. DARA, IARA and CARA give clear answers. If absolute risk aversion is not monotone, the same individual may have willingness to pay that increases over some wealth ranges and decreases over others.

Proposition 2.9 (Wealth and the maximum insurance premium) For fixed \(p\in(0,1)\) and \(S>0\), consider \(w>S\):

if \(\gamma_u\) is non-increasing, then \(\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\) is non-increasing in \(w\);
if \(\gamma_u\) is non-decreasing, then \(\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\) is non-decreasing in \(w\);
if \(\gamma_u\) is constant, then \(\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\) does not depend on \(w\).

The first two conclusions are strict when \(\gamma_u\) is decreasing or increasing, respectively.


Proof. Recall that
\[
\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)
=w-u^{-1}\!\left((1-p)u(w)+p\,u(w-S)\right).
\]
Differentiating, we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial\pi_{\max}}{\partial w}(p,S,w)
&=1-\frac{(1-p)u'(w)+p\,u'(w-S)}
{u'\!\left(w-\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\right)}\\
&=1-\frac{\mathbb E[u'(w-X)]}
{u'\!\left(w-\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\right)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
To determine the sign, introduce
\[
\varphi=u'\circ u^{-1}
\]
on \(u((0,\infty))\). Its derivative satisfies
\[
\varphi'(u(x))=\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}=-\gamma_u(x).
\]
Since \(u\) is increasing, non-increasing absolute risk aversion is equivalent to a non-decreasing derivative \(\varphi'\), hence to convexity of \(\varphi\). Jensen’s inequality then yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[u'(w-X)]
&=\mathbb E[\varphi(u(w-X))]\\
&\geq\varphi\!\left(\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\right)\\
&=u'\!\left(w-\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(\frac{\partial\pi_{\max}}{\partial w}(p,S,w)\leq0\).
If \(\gamma_u\) is non-decreasing, then \(\varphi'\) is non-increasing and \(\varphi\) is concave. Jensen’s inequality reverses, giving \(\frac{\partial\pi_{\max}}{\partial w}(p,S,w)\geq0\). If \(\gamma_u\) is constant, then \(\varphi\) is affine and the derivative is zero.
Strict monotonicity of \(\gamma_u\) makes \(\varphi\) strictly convex or strictly concave. Since \(u(w-X)\) is non-degenerate, Jensen’s inequality is then strict.







NoteAlternative proof: a wealth shift is a change of utility function





Fix \(h>0\) and define
\[
v(x)=u(x+h)
\]
for every \(x>0\). Because \(h>0\), \(v\) is a utility function on \((0,\infty)\) satisfying the same standing assumptions. Take \(w>S\), so \(w-X\geq w-S>0\) and \(w+h-X\geq w+h-S>0\). Evaluating wealth \(w+h-X\) under \(u\) is equivalent to evaluating wealth \(w-X\) under \(v\):
\[
\mathbb E[u(w+h-X)]=\mathbb E[v(w-X)].
\]
The corresponding certainty equivalents satisfy, for every \(Y>0\) almost surely with \(u(Y+h)\) integrable,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_v(Y)=\operatorname{ce}_u(Y+h)-h.
\]
Indeed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
u\!\left(\operatorname{ce}_v(Y)+h\right)
&=v\!\left(\operatorname{ce}_v(Y)\right)\\
&=\mathbb E[v(Y)]\\
&=\mathbb E[u(Y+h)]\\
&=u\!\left(\operatorname{ce}_u(Y+h)\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
and strict monotonicity of \(u\) gives the identity. Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{\max}(p,S,w+h)
&=w+h-\operatorname{ce}_u(w+h-X)\\
&=w-\operatorname{ce}_v(w-X).
\end{aligned}
\]
Now \(\gamma_v(x)=\gamma_u(x+h)\). If absolute risk aversion is non-increasing, then \(\gamma_u(x)\geq\gamma_v(x)\): by Proposition 2.6, \(u\) is an increasing concave transformation of \(v\). The ordering of certainty equivalents in Proposition 2.7 gives
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(w-X)\leq\operatorname{ce}_v(w-X),
\]
and hence
\[
\pi_{\max}(p,S,w+h)
\leq w-\operatorname{ce}_u(w-X)
=\pi_{\max}(p,S,w).
\]
Under non-decreasing absolute risk aversion the comparison reverses. Under constant absolute risk aversion it is an equality. If \(\gamma_u\) is decreasing, then \(\gamma_u(x)>\gamma_v(x)\) for every \(x\), and the strict version of Proposition 2.7 applies to the non-degenerate wealth \(w-X\): the inequality is strict. The increasing case is symmetric.



Thus, under decreasing absolute risk aversion, a wealthier individual is willing to pay less to eliminate the same monetary loss.


2.2.3 Example: CRRA utility
Let \(w>S\), \(p\in(0,1)\) and \(\rho>0\). For the CRRA utility introduced earlier,
\[
\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)=
\begin{cases}
w-\left((1-p)w^{1-\rho}+p(w-S)^{1-\rho}\right)^{1/(1-\rho)},
&\rho\neq1,\\[1.2ex]
w-w^{1-p}(w-S)^p,
&\rho=1.
\end{cases}
\]
Since \(\gamma_u(w)=\rho/w\) is decreasing, \(\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\) is decreasing in \(w\) for a fixed loss size \(S\).
For logarithmic utility, the formula becomes
\[
\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)
=w\left[1-\left(1-\frac Sw\right)^p\right].
\]
For example, if \(p=0.1\) and \(S=20\), willingness to pay is approximately \(2.21\) at \(w=100\), and \(2.10\) at \(w=200\), compared with a pure premium of \(2\).






NotePossible exercises and extensions



In this model, an interesting exercise is to study \(\pi_{\max}(p,S,w)\) as \(w\to\infty\), keeping \(p\) and \(S\) fixed: find its limit and the first correction term. Compare this with the case where the asset value is a fixed fraction of wealth, \(S=sw\) with \(s\in(0,1)\).
Also, many variants of this initial model are possible. For example, suppose damage occurs with probability \(p\), but the fraction of the asset lost is uniform on \((0,1)\). Write
\[
X=SBU,
\] where \(B\sim\mathcal B(p)\) and \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), with \(B\) and \(U\) independent, and retain \(0<S<w\). Thus \(w-X\geq w-S>0\). Then
\[
\mathbb E[u(w-X)]=(1-p)u(w)+p\int_0^1u(w-Sz)\,\mathrm dz.
\]
Use this expression to find the maximum premium for full insurance, compare it with the pure premium \(\mathbb E[X]=pS/2\), and study its dependence on wealth.




2.2.4 Proportional insurance and the safety loading
We now allow a general non-negative loss \(X\) and write
\[
m=\mathbb E[X]>0.
\]
A proportional insurance contract reimburses \(\alpha X\), where \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) is the insured fraction. Its premium is
\[
P(\alpha)=\lambda\mathbb E[\alpha X]=\lambda\alpha m,
\] where \(\lambda\geq1\).
This is a pricing assumption, often called the expected value premium principle: the price is proportional to the pure premium. It is not a definition of insurance pricing in general. Other rules can account differently for risk, expenses or capital requirements; we shall discuss premium calculation principles in Chapter 4. Here we fix this rule to study the insured’s response to prices.
The factor \(\lambda\) is the premium multiplier. Equivalently, write \(\lambda=1+\tau\), where \(\tau\geq0\) is the safety loading rate: the amount charged above the pure premium is \(\tau\alpha m\). Thus \(\lambda=1\) (or \(\tau=0\)) means actuarially fair pricing.
For the rest of this chapter, assume \(X\) is bounded and write \(M=\operatorname{ess\,sup}X\in(0,\infty)\), the smallest almost-sure upper bound on the loss. Thus \(0\leq X\leq M\) almost surely and \(0<m\leq M\). We also suppose \(u''<0\) on \((0,\infty)\).
For proportional insurance, we impose the explicit condition
\[
\boxed{w>\max\{M,\lambda m\}}.
\]
This ensures positive wealth both without insurance and with full insurance. Every intermediate coverage level also gives positive wealth, as the following bound shows.
Final wealth and expected utility are
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_\alpha&=w-X+\alpha X-\lambda\alpha m\\
&=w-(1-\alpha)X-\lambda\alpha m,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
f(\alpha)=\mathbb E[u(Y_\alpha)].
\]
Indeed,
\[
Y_\alpha=(1-\alpha)(w-X)+\alpha(w-\lambda m)
\quad\text{so}\quad
0<w-\max\{M,\lambda m\}\leq Y_\alpha\leq w.
\]
Thus \(u\), \(u'\) and \(u''\) are bounded on the fixed interval containing every \(Y_\alpha\), which justifies differentiation under expectations. The insured chooses \(\alpha\) to maximise \(f\) on \([0,1]\). All statements below about varying \(\lambda\) are made subject to \(1\leq\lambda<w/m\).
The analysis relies on a classical covariance inequality, recalled first.






NoteChebyshev’s covariance inequality and rearrangement



Two non-decreasing functions of the same random variable have non-negative covariance. More precisely, if \(a(X)\), \(b(X)\) and \(a(X)b(X)\) are integrable, then
\[
\mathbb E[a(X)b(X)]\geq\mathbb E[a(X)]\,\mathbb E[b(X)].
\]
To see this, let \(X'\) be an independent copy of \(X\). Monotonicity makes the product below non-negative. Expanding it gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
0
&\leq \mathbb E[(a(X)-a(X'))(b(X)-b(X'))]\\
&=\mathbb E[a(X)b(X)]+\mathbb E[a(X')b(X')]\\
&\quad-\mathbb E[a(X)b(X')]-\mathbb E[a(X')b(X)]\\
&=2\mathbb E[a(X)b(X)]
-2\mathbb E[a(X)]\,\mathbb E[b(X)]\\
&=2\operatorname{Cov}(a(X),b(X)).
\end{aligned}
\]
The penultimate equality uses the identical distributions for the first two terms and independence to factorise the cross terms. The inequality is strict if \(X\) is non-degenerate and both functions are strictly increasing.
The rearrangement inequality expresses a related idea: pairing two ordered sequences in the same order maximises their sum of products. If \(a_1\leq\cdots\leq a_n\) and \(b_1\leq\cdots\leq b_n\), then, for every permutation \(\sigma\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\geq\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_{\sigma(i)}.
\]
Averaging over all permutations replaces each \(b_{\sigma(i)}\) by the mean of the \(b_j\). Dividing by \(n\) gives the Chebyshev sum inequality,
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i
\geq
\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)
\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\right).
\]
This is precisely the covariance inequality applied to a uniformly chosen index.



Proposition 2.10 (Optimal proportional coverage) Suppose \(X\) is non-degenerate. The function \(f\) is strictly concave, with
\[
f'(\alpha)=\mathbb E[(X-\lambda m)u'(Y_\alpha)]
\quad\text{and}\quad
f''(\alpha)=\mathbb E[(X-\lambda m)^2u''(Y_\alpha)]<0.
\]
Define the threshold
\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{prop}}
=\frac{\mathbb E[Xu'(w-X)]}{m\,\mathbb E[u'(w-X)]}>1.
\]
Then the unique optimal insured fraction \(\alpha^*\) satisfies:

if \(\lambda=1\), then \(\alpha^*=1\);
if \(1<\lambda<\lambda_{\mathrm{prop}}\), then \(\alpha^*\in(0,1)\) is the unique solution of \(f'(\alpha^*)=0\);
if \(\lambda\geq\lambda_{\mathrm{prop}}\), then \(\alpha^*=0\).

In particular, full proportional insurance is never optimal when \(\lambda>1\).


Proof. For each realisation of \(X\), \(Y_\alpha\) is affine in \(\alpha\), so concavity of \(u\) implies concavity of \(f\). Differentiation gives the displayed formulas. Non-degeneracy of \(X\) and \(u''<0\) make the second derivative strictly negative.
At zero coverage,
\[
f'(0)
=\mathbb E[Xu'(w-X)]-\lambda m\,\mathbb E[u'(w-X)]
=m\,\mathbb E[u'(w-X)](\lambda_{\mathrm{prop}}-\lambda).
\]
Both \(x\mapsto x\) and \(x\mapsto u'(w-x)\) are increasing. The strict covariance inequality in the preceding note therefore gives
\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{prop}}
=1+\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,u'(w-X))}
{m\,\mathbb E[u'(w-X)]}>1.
\]
At full coverage, final wealth is the constant \(w-\lambda m\), hence
\[
f'(1)=(1-\lambda)m\,u'(w-\lambda m).
\]
This is zero when \(\lambda=1\) and strictly negative when \(\lambda>1\). Since \(f'\) is decreasing, its endpoint signs give all three cases.

The last statement of Proposition 2.10 is known as Mossin’s theorem (Mossin 1968).
The covariance term expresses the value of insurance: reimbursement arrives in states where losses are high and marginal utility of wealth is high. A safety loading reduces this benefit by charging more than the expected reimbursement.
At full insurance, however, marginal utility is the same in every state. A first-order argument in \(\varepsilon>0\) explains the incentive to reduce coverage: moving from \(1\) to \(1-\varepsilon\) saves \(\lambda\varepsilon m\) in premium and introduces a retained loss of mean \(\varepsilon m\). More precisely,
\[
f(1-\varepsilon)-f(1)
=\varepsilon(\lambda-1)m\,u'(w-\lambda m)+O(\varepsilon^2).
\]
For \(\lambda>1\), the gain in expected wealth is first order, while the utility cost of the small risk around sure wealth is only second order. This is why paying more than one euro per expected euro reimbursed cannot justify eliminating the very last part of the risk. Figure 2.2 illustrates the three regimes of Proposition 2.10.








Figure 2.2: Expected utility under proportional insurance. All panels use the same vertical scale. Logarithmic utility, initial wealth 100, and a loss of 40 with probability 0.2.







2.2.5 Choosing the shape of insurance: deductibles
Proportional insurance is only one possible contract. For the rest of the chapter, we strengthen the wealth condition to the simple sufficient inequality
\[
\boxed{w>M+\lambda m}.
\]
This allows us to compare all the indemnities below without imposing an additional solvency constraint on each contract. We now allow any measurable indemnity function \(I\) satisfying
\[
0\leq I(x)\leq x
\quad\text{for}\quad
x\geq0.
\]
Thus the insurer never pays a negative amount and never reimburses more than the loss. These constraints alone permit a wide variety of shapes, including non-monotone indemnities. Figure 2.3 shows both familiar contracts and less conventional admissible examples.








Figure 2.3: Examples of admissible indemnities. Every curve lies between zero and the dashed full-insurance line I(x) = x. The last two satisfy the constraints although reimbursement need not increase with the loss.





We keep the expected value premium principle introduced above, with the same multiplier \(\lambda\) for every contract:
\[
P(I)=\lambda\mathbb E[I(X)].
\]
The insured seeks to maximise
\[
F(I)=\mathbb E\!\left[u\bigl(w-X+I(X)-\lambda\mathbb E[I(X)]\bigr)\right].
\]
For every such contract, \(0\leq\mathbb E[I(X)]\leq m\), and hence
\[
0<w-M-\lambda m
\leq w-X+I(X)-\lambda\mathbb E[I(X)]\leq w.
\]
All final wealth levels therefore lie in the same positive interval \([w-M-\lambda m,w]\). The condition \(w>M+\lambda m\) is sufficient but not necessary for each individual contract.
Here \(F\) is a functional: its input is a function \(I\), rather than a real number. The admissible indemnities form a convex subset of an infinite-dimensional function space.
Optimisation over functions often uses the calculus of variations. A classical source of the subject is the brachistochrone problem, posed by Johann Bernoulli in 1696: among curves connecting two points, find the one along which a particle descends under gravity in the shortest time. Euler and Lagrange subsequently developed systematic methods for such problems. Here the unknown function is an indemnity rather than a trajectory. In what follows, we need only the elementary variational idea of moving from one function towards another and differentiating along that direction.
A deductible contract with deductible \(D\geq0\) has indemnity
\[
I_D(x)=(x-D)_+,
\] where \((z)_+=\max(z,0)\).
The individual pays losses up to \(D\), and the insurer pays the excess. Final wealth is therefore
\[
Y_D=w-X+(X-D)_+-\lambda\mathbb E[(X-D)_+].
\]
In particular, it equals \(w-X-P(I_D)\) when \(X\leq D\), and \(w-D-P(I_D)\) when \(X>D\).
Our strategy has two steps. Given any contract \(I\), we first find a deductible contract \(I_D\) with the same premium. We then show that this deductible contract gives at least as much expected utility. This will reduce the choice of an entire indemnity function to the choice of the single number \(D\).

Proposition 2.11 (Matching the pure premium with a deductible) For every admissible indemnity \(I\), there exists \(D\in[0,M]\) such that
\[
\mathbb E[(X-D)_+]=\mathbb E[I(X)].
\]
If \(\mathbb E[I(X)]>0\), then this deductible is unique and belongs to \([0,M)\). If \(\mathbb E[I(X)]=0\), then the contract pays nothing almost surely; any \(D\geq M\) gives the same zero indemnity, and we may choose \(D=M\).


Proof. The function
\[
H(D)=\mathbb E[(X-D)_+]
\]
is continuous: the inequality \(|(x-D)_+-(x-E)_+|\leq|D-E|\) gives \(|H(D)-H(E)|\leq|D-E|\). Moreover,
\[
H(0)=m
\quad\text{and}\quad
H(M)=0.
\]
Since \(0\leq\mathbb E[I(X)]\leq m\), existence follows from the intermediate value theorem.
For uniqueness, recall that \(M\) is the smallest almost-sure upper bound on \(X\). If \(0\leq D_1<D_2<M\), then \(\mathbb P(X>D_2)>0\), and on \(\{ X>D_2\}\) the two indemnities differ by \(D_2-D_1\). Hence \(H(D_1)>H(D_2)\). Also \(H(D)>0\) for \(D<M\), so a positive target expectation is attained at exactly one deductible. Finally, a non-negative indemnity with zero expectation vanishes almost surely, as does \((X-D)_+\) for every \(D\geq M\).


Theorem 2.2 (Optimality of deductible insurance) Let \(I\) be any admissible indemnity and choose \(D\in[0,M]\) such that
\[
\mathbb E[I_D(X)]=\mathbb E[I(X)].
\]
Then the two contracts have the same premium and
\[
F(I_D)\geq F(I).
\]
The inequality is strict if \(\mathbb P(I_D(X)\neq I(X))>0\). Consequently, maximising expected utility over all admissible indemnities reduces to choosing a deductible \(D\in[0,M]\).


Proof. Write
\[
P=\lambda\mathbb E[I(X)]=\lambda\mathbb E[I_D(X)]
\quad\text{and}\quad
\Delta(x)=I(x)-I_D(x).
\]
Interpolate between the two contracts:
\[
J_\theta=I_D+\theta(I-I_D)
\quad\text{for}\quad
\theta\in[0,1].
\]
Every \(J_\theta\) is admissible and has premium \(P\), since \(\mathbb E[\Delta(X)]=0\). Define
\[
g(\theta)=F(J_\theta)
=\mathbb E[u(w-X+J_\theta(X)-P)].
\]
For each realised loss, final wealth is affine in \(\theta\) and lies in \([w-M-\lambda m,w]\). Thus \(g\) is concave; boundedness of \(u'\) on this interval justifies differentiation under the expectation, giving
\[
g'(0)=\mathbb E[u'(w-X+(X-D)_+-P)\Delta(X)].
\]
Split the expectation according to whether the loss exceeds the deductible:
\[
\begin{aligned}
g'(0)
&=\mathbb E\!\left[u'(w-X-P)\Delta(X)\mathbf 1_{\{X\leq D\}}\right]\\
&\quad+u'(w-D-P)\mathbb E\!\left[\Delta(X)\mathbf 1_{\{X>D\}}\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Using \(\mathbf 1_{\{X>D\}}=1-\mathbf 1_{\{X\leq D\}}\) and \(\mathbb E[\Delta(X)]=0\),
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[\Delta(X)\mathbf 1_{\{X>D\}}\right]
=-\mathbb E\!\left[\Delta(X)\mathbf 1_{\{X\leq D\}}\right].
\]
On \(\{X\leq D\}\), the deductible pays nothing, so \(\Delta(X)=I(X)\geq0\). Since \(u'\) is decreasing and \(w-X-P\geq w-D-P\) on this event, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
&g'(0)\\
&=\mathbb E\Bigl[
\underbrace{\bigl(u'(w-X-P)-u'(w-D-P)\bigr)}_{\leq0\text{ on }\{X\leq D\}}\\
&\qquad\times\underbrace{\mathbf 1_{\{X\leq D\}}\,I(X)}_{\geq0}
\Bigr]\\
&\leq0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Concavity now gives
\[
F(I)=g(1)\leq g(0)+g'(0)\leq g(0)=F(I_D).
\]
If \(\Delta(X)\) is non-zero with positive probability, strict concavity of \(u\) makes \(g\) strictly concave. Its tangent inequality at zero is then strict at one, proving strict preference.

This result is due to Arrow (Arrow 1963, 1971).
For a fixed expected reimbursement, insurance is most valuable in states where the insured would otherwise be poorest. A deductible directs reimbursement towards large losses and equalises final wealth across all losses exceeding the deductible. Covering small losses instead uses part of the same premium to transfer money into states where marginal utility is lower.


2.2.6 Choosing the optimal deductible
The remaining problem is a standard one-dimensional maximisation:
\[
\max_{D\in[0,M]}\psi(D),
\] where \[
\psi(D)=F(I_D)
=\mathbb E\!\left[
u\!\left(w-X+(X-D)_+-\lambda\mathbb E[(X-D)_+]\right)
\right].
\]
The function \(\psi\) is continuous on \([0,M]\): the indemnities \((X-D)_+\) and the premium \(\lambda H(D)\) vary continuously with \(D\), and final wealth stays in \([w-M-\lambda m,w]\), where \(u\) is bounded, so dominated convergence applies. Compactness of \([0,M]\) then guarantees that an optimal deductible \(D^*\) exists, and by Theorem 2.2 the contract \(I_{D^*}\) is optimal among all admissible indemnities.
Final wealth can also be written \(Y_D=w-\min(X,D)-\lambda H(D)\), with \(H(D)=\mathbb E[(X-D)_+]\) as before. As \(h\downarrow0\), \((\min(X,D+h)-\min(X,D))/h\to\mathbf 1_{\{X>D\}}\) and \((H(D+h)-H(D))/h\to-\mathbb P(X>D)\), with difference quotients bounded by \(1\). Since \(u'\) is bounded on \([w-M-\lambda m,w]\), dominated convergence gives the right derivative
\[
\psi'_+(D)
=\lambda\,\mathbb P(X>D)\,\mathbb E[u'(Y_D)]
-\mathbb E\!\left[u'(Y_D)\mathbf 1_{\{X>D\}}\right]
\quad\text{for}\quad
D\in[0,M).
\]
The first term is the marginal expected-utility benefit of the premium saving from raising the deductible; the second is the marginal utility cost of the extra retained loss, which falls precisely in the states where wealth is lowest. This yields the deductible counterpart of Mossin’s theorem.

Proposition 2.12 (Optimal deductible and safety loading) Let \(x_{\min}=\operatorname{ess\,inf}X\in[0,M]\).

If \(\lambda=1\), the deductible \(D=0\) (full insurance) is optimal. More precisely, \(D\in[0,M]\) is optimal if and only if \(D\leq x_{\min}\); all these deductibles give the same sure wealth \(w-m\). In particular, \(D=0\) is the unique optimal deductible when \(x_{\min}=0\), for instance when \(\mathbb P(X=0)>0\).
If \(\lambda>1\), every optimal deductible satisfies \(D^*>0\): full insurance is never optimal.



Proof. Suppose \(\lambda=1\). For every \(D\),
\[
\mathbb E[Y_D]
=w-\mathbb E[\min(X,D)]-\mathbb E[(X-D)_+]
=w-m,
\]
since \(\min(x,D)+(x-D)_+=x\). Jensen’s inequality gives \(\psi(D)\leq u(w-m)=\psi(0)\), so \(D=0\) is optimal. If \(D\leq x_{\min}\), then \(\min(X,D)=D\) almost surely and \(Y_D=w-m\) is constant. If \(D>x_{\min}\), then \(\min(X,D)\) is non-degenerate: it cannot equal \(D\) almost surely, since \(\mathbb P(X<D)>0\), and it cannot equal a constant \(c<D\) almost surely, since then \(X=c\) almost surely and \(M=c<D\). Strict concavity of \(u\) then gives \(\psi(D)<\psi(0)\).
Suppose \(\lambda>1\). At \(D=0\), final wealth is the constant \(w-\lambda m\), so
\[
\psi'_+(0)=(\lambda-1)\,\mathbb P(X>0)\,u'(w-\lambda m)>0,
\]
because \(\mathbb P(X>0)>0\) when \(m>0\). Hence \(\psi(D)>\psi(0)\) for all sufficiently small \(D>0\), and \(D=0\) is not optimal.

As with proportional coverage, a positive loading makes it optimal to retain part of the risk. Raising the deductible from \(0\) to a small \(h>0\) saves \(\lambda\mathbb E[\min(X,h)]\) in premium but also introduces an expected retained loss of \(\mathbb E[\min(X,h)]\). The net gain in expected wealth is therefore \((\lambda-1)\mathbb E[\min(X,h)]\), which is first order in \(h\). The utility cost of the additional uncertainty around expected wealth is only second order. It is the saving on the loading, after accounting for the expected retained loss, that makes a small deductible attractive.
To characterise candidate optimal deductibles, observe that \(Y_D=w-D-\lambda H(D)\) on \(\{X>D\}\). The right derivative therefore factors as
\[
\psi'_+(D)
=\mathbb P(X>D)
\left[\lambda\mathbb E[u'(Y_D)]-u'\!\left(w-D-\lambda H(D)\right)\right]
\quad\text{for}\quad
D\in[0,M).
\]
The same dominated-convergence argument, now taking difference quotients from the left, gives
\[
\psi'_-(D)
=\mathbb P(X\geq D)
\left[\lambda\mathbb E[u'(Y_D)]-u'\!\left(w-D-\lambda H(D)\right)\right]
\quad\text{for}\quad
D\in(0,M].
\]
Indeed, the left derivatives of \(\min(X,D)\) and \(H(D)\) are \(\mathbf 1_{\{X\geq D\}}\) and \(-\mathbb P(X\geq D)\), respectively, and \(Y_D=w-D-\lambda H(D)\) also on \(\{X=D\}\).
At a local maximum \(D\in(0,M)\), we must have \(\psi'_-(D)\geq0\) and \(\psi'_+(D)\leq0\). Since \(\mathbb P(X>D)>0\) for \(D<M\), both probability factors are strictly positive. The common bracket must therefore vanish:
\[
\lambda\mathbb E[u'(Y_D)]
=u'\!\left(w-D-\lambda H(D)\right).
\]
This condition remains valid when the loss distribution has an atom at \(D\). In fact, it is also sufficient for global optimality. The relevant concavity is that of expected utility as a function of the indemnity, rather than as a function of the deductible.

Proposition 2.13 (A sufficient condition for an optimal deductible) Under the standing assumptions of this section, suppose that \(D\in(0,M)\) satisfies
\[
\lambda\mathbb E[u'(Y_D)]
=u'\!\left(w-D-\lambda H(D)\right).
\]
Then \(I_D(x)=(x-D)_+\) maximises expected utility among all admissible indemnities \(0\leq I(x)\leq x\).
If \(\lambda>1\), the optimal indemnity is unique up to almost-sure equality, and the optimal deductible in \([0,M]\) is unique.


Proof. Let
\[
c=w-D-\lambda H(D)
\quad\text{and}\quad
k=\lambda\mathbb E[u'(Y_D)]=u'(c).
\]
For any admissible indemnity \(I\), put \(\Delta=I(X)-I_D(X)\). The corresponding final wealth differs from \(Y_D\) by \(\Delta-\lambda\mathbb E[\Delta]\). The tangent inequality for the concave function \(u\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(I)-F(I_D)
&\leq\mathbb E\!\left[u'(Y_D)
\bigl(\Delta-\lambda\mathbb E[\Delta]\bigr)\right]\\
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\bigl(u'(Y_D)-k\bigr)\Delta\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
On \(\{X>D\}\), final wealth equals \(c\), so the coefficient \(u'(Y_D)-k\) is zero. On \(\{X\leq D\}\), we have \(Y_D\geq c\) and hence \(u'(Y_D)-k\leq0\), while \(\Delta=I(X)\geq0\). Therefore \(F(I)-F(I_D)\leq0\).
For uniqueness when \(\lambda>1\), observe that the admissible set of indemnities is convex and final wealth depends affinely on the indemnity. Moreover, if two indemnities \(I\) and \(J\) give the same final wealth almost surely, then
\[
I(X)-J(X)=\lambda\mathbb E[I(X)-J(X)]
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
Taking expectations and using \(\lambda>1\) shows that both sides are zero. Strict concavity of \(u\) thus makes \(F\) strictly concave in the indemnity, up to almost-sure equality. Its maximiser is unique. Finally, distinct deductibles in \([0,M]\) give distinct indemnities with positive probability, because \(M=\operatorname{ess\,sup}X\). This proves uniqueness of the optimal deductible.

The sufficiency argument has a direct economic interpretation. Above the deductible, marginal utility is constant and equals the marginal expected-utility cost of the premium. Below the deductible, marginal utility is lower, so adding reimbursement there cannot improve expected utility at the stated price. Concavity makes this marginal comparison sufficient for a global conclusion.
For \(\lambda>1\), there can consequently be at most one solution of the first-order condition in \((0,M)\). If such a solution exists, it is the unique optimal deductible. If there is no interior solution, existence of an optimum and the exclusion of \(D=0\) imply that the optimum is \(D=M\), corresponding to no insurance. The actuarially fair case \(\lambda=1\) was characterised in Proposition 2.12.






NoteIs expected utility concave in the deductible?





Not in general. Consider \(u(y)=\log y\), \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(w=2\) and \(\lambda=6/5\). These choices satisfy all the standing assumptions. For \(D\in[0,1]\), write
\[
H(D)=\frac{(1-D)^2}{2}.
\]
Also set
\[
A_D=2-\frac35(1-D)^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
c_D=A_D-D.
\]
Direct integration gives
\[
\psi(D)=\int_0^D\log(A_D-x)\,\mathrm dx+(1-D)\log c_D
\]
and
\[
\psi'(D)=(1-D)\left[
\frac65\log\!\left(\frac{A_D}{c_D}\right)
+\frac{\frac65(1-D)-1}{c_D}
\right].
\]
Differentiating once more yields
\[
\lim_{D\uparrow1}\psi''(D)
=1-\frac65\log2>0.
\]
Thus \(\psi\) is strictly convex near \(D=1\). Nevertheless, solving the first-order condition gives the unique global optimum
\[
D^*\simeq0.751167
\quad\text{and}\quad
\lambda H(D^*)\simeq0.037151.
\]
For comparison, \(\psi(0)\simeq0.336472\), \(\psi(D^*)\simeq0.387697\) and \(\psi(1)\simeq0.386294\). Optimality follows from the proposition, rather than from these numerical comparisons.

title: Microeconomics of insurance
text:
Key takeaways







Under expected utility, preferences are represented by \(\mathbb E[u(X)]\), with \(u\) determined up to an increasing affine transformation. Concavity of \(u\) expresses risk aversion through Jensen’s inequality.
The certainty equivalent \(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)=u^{-1}(\mathbb E[u(X)])\) never exceeds \(\mathbb E[X]\); the gap is the risk premium. For a small risk it is approximately \(\frac12\gamma_u(\mathbb E[X])\,\mathbb V(X)\), and exactly so for CARA utility and Gaussian risk.
The coefficient of absolute risk aversion \(\gamma_u=-u''/u'\) compares agents: \(\gamma_u\geq\gamma_v\) everywhere exactly when \(u\) is an increasing concave transformation of \(v\), and then every certainty equivalent under \(u\) is no higher than under \(v\).
A risk-averse individual is willing to pay more than the pure premium for full insurance, by exactly the risk premium of uninsured wealth. Whether this willingness to pay rises or falls with wealth depends on how \(\gamma_u\) varies: it falls under DARA, is constant under CARA and rises under IARA.
When the premium is \(\lambda\) times the expected indemnity, full proportional coverage is optimal for \(\lambda=1\) and never optimal for \(\lambda>1\) (Mossin’s theorem); for \(\lambda\geq\lambda_{\mathrm{prop}}\), no coverage is bought at all.
Among all indemnities with \(0\leq I(x)\leq x\) and the same premium, a deductible contract gives the highest expected utility (Arrow). Choosing a contract reduces to choosing a single number \(D\).
With a positive loading, the optimal deductible is strictly positive. An interior deductible is characterised by \(\lambda\mathbb E[u'(Y_D)]=u'(w-D-\lambda H(D))\), a condition that is also sufficient even though expected utility need not be concave in \(D\).
